sens: Make a decision as a magistrate or judicial authority
Examine and resolve a dispute or accusation
Evaluate, assess the good or the evil
H8200.detail:
1. To judge primarily means to exercise an official function: to render justice, like a magistrate who examines a case and pronounces a judgment. In Ezra 7:25, Ezra is commanded to appoint judges who will administer justice to the citizens of Persia according to God's laws — this is the image of the judge sitting who weighs the evidence and decides.
2. The word can also refer to the action of examining and deciding between two conflicting parties, discerning right from wrong — this is judging a quarrel or a lawsuit.
3. In a figurative sense, to judge means to evaluate the moral value or quality of something, forming a judgment about someone's goodness or guilt.
H8200.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁפַט (shephat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of separating, distinguishing, deciding — hence the image of the judge who separates right from wrong. The root generates several words in the family: שִׁפְטוּ (let them judge), שׁוֹפְטִים (the judges, notably from the book of Judges). It is a very common verb in biblical Hebrew to denote the act of judging.
H8200.emploi: The verb shephat appears 198 times in the Old Testament. It is used to describe the actions of the judges of Israel (the book of Judges), those of kings, and those of God Himself who judges the peoples and hearts. In Ezra 7:25, it is used in the participle to refer to the judges that the Persian king allows Ezra to appoint — the context is that of the Persian judicial administration in favor of the Jews returned from exile. The word covers both civil judgment and religious or moral judgment.
H8200.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that judgment is primarily a responsibility entrusted by God to those who govern and administer justice according to His law. It also evokes that God alone is the supreme judge of hearts, and that believers must be careful not to judge with arrogance, but with wisdom and fairness.

sens: The decision rendered by an authority when judging a case
The act of judging, exercising the authority of justice
The punishment that God inflicts on His people or His enemies
The visible and terrible manifestation of God's power in history
H8201.detail:
1. Judgment is primarily the decision rendered by one who has authority: it is the verdict, the sentence that determines what is just. This is what a judge or a king renders after examining a case (Proverbs 19:29 speaks of punishments reserved for mockers, that is, judgments that strike them).
2. Next, the word designates the act of judging itself, the exercise of the power of justice: God "executes His judgments" against His enemies or against His unfaithful people (Ezekiel 5:10, 11:9). It is the ongoing action, not just the spoken word.
3. Judgment also becomes the concrete and visible punishment: the ten plagues of Egypt are called "judgments" because they manifest God's sentence against Pharaoh and his gods (Exodus 6:6, 12:12). God's justice does not remain abstract — it is executed in reality, harshly.
4. At the deepest level, God's judgments are acts that reveal His sovereignty over nations and history. When God executes His judgments, He shows that He is the master, and the peoples see and recognize His authority (Ezekiel 5:15, 25:11).
H8201.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁפֶט (shephet) comes from a root that means "to judge," "to decide." The root is related to the idea of rendering a definitive decision, separating the just from the unjust. The corresponding verb appears throughout the Bible, notably in descriptions of the "judges" of Israel (the leaders who governed the people before the kings). The word thus evokes the authority that observes, evaluates, and pronounces — an action that transfers the will of the judge into reality.
H8201.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the prophetic books (Ezekiel 8 times) and in the narratives of the Pentateuch. Its meaning slightly changes depending on the context. In Exodus, the "judgments" are the plagues that strike Egypt: they manifest God's condemnation against Pharaoh who oppresses Israel. In the prophets, especially Ezekiel, judgment becomes a widespread punishment against Jerusalem or against the nations (Egypt, Tyre) that have offended the Lord: destruction, captivity, death. Sometimes, as in 2 Chronicles 24:24, judgment is the human execution of a sentence, when the Syrians "execute justice" on King Joash. Each time, the word designates an action whose terrible effects are seen or felt.
H8201.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God's justice is never distant or theoretical: it is executed in history and in our lives. It also invites a fear of the Lord — not out of panic, but out of clear reverence. Those who read these texts about God's judgments see that rebellion against Him has real and visible consequences. It is also a relief for those who suffer: God does not forget injustices, and He will render justice in His time.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Simeon sent to scout the promised land
Father of the prophet Elisha
Descendant of Zerubbabel in the royal line of Judah
Leader of the tribe of Gad
H8202G.detail:
1. Shaphat, son of Hori, is one of the twelve men chosen by Moses to explore the land of Canaan before the conquest (Numbers 13:5). He represents the tribe of Simeon and participates in this decisive mission that will last forty days.
2. In the Old Testament, Shaphat is also known as the father of the great prophet Elisha, who will succeed the prophet Elijah.
3. Another Shaphat appears among the descendants of Zerubbabel, fitting into the royal line of Judah after the Babylonian exile.
4. An additional Shaphat is mentioned as the leader of the tribe of Gad, holding a position of responsibility.
5. Finally, a Shaphat son of Adlai served as chief shepherd for David, overseeing the flocks in the valleys.
H8202G.origine: The name Shaphat comes from the Hebrew root שפט (shaphat), which means "to judge" or "to render judgment." The name thus suggests the idea of "he has judged" or one who exercises discernment authority. It is an active nominal form of the verb, common in Hebrew onomastics for forming theophoric names or expressing a desired quality.
H8202G.emploi: Shaphat is a name borne by at least five distinct characters in the Hebrew Bible. The only one directly mentioned in the provided usages is the son of Hori, prince of Simeon, cited in Numbers 13:5 during the sending of the twelve scouts. This passage is crucial for understanding who Shaphat was: one of those who saw the land of Canaan before Israel's definitive entry. The other Shaphats mentioned in the source definition (father of Elisha, descendant of Zerubbabel, leader of Gad, shepherd of David) do not appear in the provided Segond usage, but they testify to the importance of the name in Israel's history.

sens: father of the prophet Elisha
landowner and head of a family in Israel during the divided monarchy
H8202H.detail:
1. Shaphat is the father of the prophet Elisha, first mentioned when the Lord commands Elijah to anoint him as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19:16). He is a man from Judah, living in Abel-Mehola, whose son will become one of the greatest prophets of Israel.
2. Shaphat was a wealthy landowner: his son Elisha was plowing with twelve pairs of oxen, which shows that the family was rich and influential (1 Kings 19:19). His sufficiently high social status allowed Elisha to become a servant of the prophet Elijah and then a prophet himself.
H8202H.origine: The name Shaphat means "he has judged" or "he judged" in Hebrew, formed from the root of the verb "to judge" (shaphat). It is a theophoric name, expressing the action of God who judges. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but the provided usages specifically refer to the father of Elisha.
H8202H.emploi: Shaphat appears four times in the Bible, always in the context of the prophet Elisha. He is first mentioned during his anointing (1 Kings 19:16), then when Elijah encounters him plowing (1 Kings 19:19). The other two occurrences simply designate him as the father of Elisha (2 Kings 3:11 and 2 Kings 6:31), in critical moments when the prophet is being sought or threatened. Shaphat himself never figures prominently: he is known only through his connection to the illustrious prophet Elisha.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, descendant of Zerubbabel in the royal lineage
H8202I.detail: Schaphath is a man of the people of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:22. He is a son of Schemaiah and a descendant of Zerubbabel, who was governor of Judah during the return from exile. He is part of the royal genealogy of Judah, the line of David's kings.
H8202I.origine: The name Schaphath comes from the Hebrew root שׁפַט (shaphat), which means "to judge" or "he has judged." This verb evokes the authority and responsibility of one who administers justice. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including the father of the prophet Elisha and a prince of Simeon who was sent to explore the promised land. The name carries the idea of governance and judgment.
H8202I.emploi: Schaphath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:22, where he is named among the six sons of Schemaiah. This passage lists the descendants of Zerubbabel and maintains the thread of the royal genealogy of Judah after the Babylonian exile. His brief mention suggests that he had a recognized place in the lineage, even though no particular act is reported of him.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H8202J.detail: 1. Schaphath is a chief of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 5:12, where he is listed among the principal members of his tribe at the time when Israel was divided into two kingdoms.
H8202J.origine: The Hebrew name Schaphath literally means "he has judged" or "judged," formed from the root שׁפט (shaphat), which means "to judge." This name expresses the act of administering justice, which was an honor and an important charge for the leaders of Israel. Several characters in the Old Testament bear this name, including the father of the prophet Elisha and one of the spies sent by Moses.
H8202J.emploi: Schaphath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:12. He is cited as one of the chiefs of the tribe of Gad, alongside Joel and Jaenaï. This succinct mention is part of a genealogical list that records the important families of Gad during the divided monarchy, when these tribes lived in Transjordan. The context suggests that he was a person of authority and responsibility in his community.

sens: Son of Adlai, overseer of King David's royal herds
H8202K.detail: 1. Schaphath is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the role of overseer of King David's cattle herds. He was responsible for overseeing the oxen and livestock that the king owned in the valleys, an important function in an economy where wealth was measured in herds (1 Chronicles 27:29).
H8202K.origine: The name Schaphath comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to judge" or "to administer justice" (the verb שׁפַט shophat). The name would thus literally mean "he has judged" or "the one who judges." This name belongs to a family of common words in biblical Hebrew: we find notably the verb shophat (to judge) and the noun shophet (judge), the latter designating the leaders of the Israelites before the establishment of the monarchy.
H8202K.emploi: Schaphath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:29, in an administrative list established by King David enumerating the overseers of his property and herds. The text presents him as "son of Adlai" and as "chief of the oxen in the valleys," indicating that he was an officer of the royal household, responsible for managing the royal cattle grazing in the lowland pastures. This is a detail of the organization of the kingdom, reflecting the importance of livestock as a source of wealth and royal prestige.

sens: Son of David and Abital, fifth son of King David
H8203G.detail: Schephathia is one of the sons born to David during his reign in Hebron, before he became king over all Israel. He is the son of David and Abital, and appears in the list of the king's children (2 Samuel 3:4 and 1 Chronicles 3:3). He is the fifth son of David listed in these genealogies.
H8203G.origine: The name Schephathia means "Jehovah has judged." It is formed from two Hebrew elements: "Jehovah" (the divine name) and a term meaning "to judge" or "to administer justice." This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the royal children of Israel, expressing a trust in God's justice and judgment.
H8203G.emploi: Schephathia is mentioned twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages that list the sons of David born in Hebron. He appears in the official list of David's royal children with their respective mothers (2 Samuel 3:4 and 1 Chronicles 3:3). These two references confirm his rank as the fifth son of King David.

sens: Descendant of Reuel and father of Meshullam, mentioned during the return from Babylonian exile
H8203H.detail: Schephathia is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, but this one is specifically identified in 1 Chronicles 9:8 as the son of Reuel and the father of Meshullam. He appears in the genealogy of the Judeans who returned from Babylonian captivity to reinhabit Jerusalem. His name means "The Lord has judged," which reminds us that God was the one who governed the return and restoration of His people after the exile.
H8203H.origine: The name Schephathia (Hebrew שְׁפַטְיָהוּ) is composed of two elements: "shaphat" which means "to judge" and "Yahu" which is a form of the divine name "Jehovah" (the Lord). The theophoric names of this type, which incorporate the name of God, were common in Israel and expressed the faith confession of the parents regarding what God was accomplishing or could accomplish. Several men bore this name at different times in Israel's history.
H8203H.emploi: Schephathia is mentioned only once in the provided usage: in 1 Chronicles 9:8, where he is presented as the son of Reuel and the father of Meshullam, in the list of Judeans who resettled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Although the recorded biblical text retains only this specific occurrence, the name was borne by at least eight different individuals throughout Israel's history, from the time of King David to the period of the return from exile. This shows the popularity and importance of this name in Israelite tradition.

sens: Man of the divided monarchy in Israel
Mighty warrior of David, from the family of the Haruphites
H8203I.detail:
1. Schéphathia is a character from the Old Testament living at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. The name means in Hebrew "Yahweh has judged" — an expression of trust in divine justice.
2. More specifically, he is one of the renowned warriors of David who joined him at Ziklag, bearing the title of Haruphite — that is, belonging to the family or clan of the Haruphites (1 Chronicles 12:5).
H8203I.origine: The name Schéphathia is composed of two Hebrew elements: "shephat" (judged, from the verb meaning to judge or render a judgment) and "yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh). This type of theophoric name — which carries the name of God — expresses the faith confession of the parents who recognize that God judges with justice. The same root is found in other biblical names such as Schéphéla or the title of judge (shophet).
H8203I.emploi: Schéphathia appears only in 1 Chronicles 12:5 in the Segond 1910. He is mentioned among the valiant warriors who joined David at Ziklag, listed alongside Eluzai, Jerimoth, and Bealiah. This enumeration is part of a list of warriors from various origins and clans who recognized David as the legitimate king and supported him during his years of flight, before he became king of Israel.
H8203I.portee: This name reminds us that even great warriors and supporters of the king are, ultimately, under God's judgment. The presence of Schéphathia among David's warriors illustrates how God gathers faithful men around the king He has chosen.

sens: Son of Maacah and prince of the tribe of Simeon during the time of King David
H8203J.detail: This name refers to a figure in the Old Testament who lived during the time of the divided monarchy. He was the son of Maacah and held the position of chief or prince of the tribe of Simeon. The Bible mentions him only once, in 1 Chronicles 27:16, where he is listed among the leaders of the tribes of Israel in service to King David.
H8203J.origine: The name Schephathia means "Jehovah has judged," composed of two elements: the divine name Jah (God) and the verb shaphat which means "to judge." It is a theonym, a name that incorporates the name or an attribute of God. Several figures bear this name in the Old Testament, which was common in Israel to convey a religious conviction in the very name of the children.
H8203J.emploi: Schephathia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:16, where the text lists the leaders of the twelve tribes of Israel. At that time, he is the official representative of the tribe of Simeon, appointed by King David or recognized as such. His inclusion in this administrative list shows his status as an important tribal leader.

sens: Son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, during the time of the divided monarchy
H8203K.detail: 1. Schephathia is one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy when the kingdom of Israel was split between north and south. The text of 2 Chronicles 21:2 mentions him as the brother of Joram, who became king after Jehoshaphat, and of several other princes: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, and Michael. All were sons of the king.
H8203K.origine: The name Schephathia means "the Lord has judged" in Hebrew: it combines the divine name (Yah) and the root of the verb "to judge" (shaphat). This name expresses the conviction that God exercises His judgment and justice. It is a typical name of the Judah monarchy, where theophoric names (containing the name of God) were common.
H8203K.emploi: Schephathia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 21:2. He appears in the list of the sons of Jehoshaphat listed before the account of Joram's succession to the throne. Although he is a prince of royal lineage, the Bible does not report any particular deeds of his life. His existence shows that Jehoshaphat had several sons, but only Joram received the royal charge — which followed the custom of the time.
H8203K.portee: The discreet mention of Schephathia reminds us that many biblical figures, even of high birth, remain in the shadows of history. It also emphasizes that God's grace and role in His plan do not depend on prestige or social position: only Joram was chosen to reign, while the other sons, despite their royal blood, disappear from the narratives. It is a lesson in humility.

sens: Descendant of a family of exiles returned from Babylon
Head of a family among the exiles of the return
H8203L.detail:
1. Schephathia is the name of an important family among the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. Its original meaning, "Jehovah has judged," reminds us that this name proclaims divine action. The family is mentioned in Ezra 2:4 and Nehemiah 7:9 with exactly three hundred seventy-two descendants, indicating a prosperous and well-established lineage.

2. A notable member of this family, Zebadiah son of Michael, is specifically designated as the head of the family (Ezra 8:8) at the time of the later return of the exiles with Ezra. This detail highlights the leadership role that this family exercised among those who were rebuilding the Jewish community after the captivity.
H8203L.origine: The name Schephathia combines the Hebrew "shafat" (to judge) and the divine name "Yahu" (Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God and expresses a religious conviction: the one who bears it or their family recognizes that God judges. Many Hebrew names from this period follow this pattern, confessing a truth about God's character or action.
H8203L.emploi: Schephathia designates a family of exiles returned from Babylon during the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra (around the 5th century B.C.). It appears three times in the provided usages: first as an important house counting 372 descendants (Ezra 2:4 and Nehemiah 7:9, with the exact same number), then in the person of Zebadiah his son, who led the later contingent of his family (Ezra 8:8). This genealogical and numerical stability suggests a preserved and prosperous lineage in the renewal of Israel.
H8203L.portee: For the Christian reader, the repeated mention of Schephathia reminds us that God never loses sight of His people, even in exile. The name itself proclaims that "Jehovah has judged" — this judgment leads to restoration and return. It is an assurance that God's promises remain active even in the midst of trial and dispersion.

sens: Head of a family of exiles returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel
H8203M.detail: 1. Schephathia is a name borne by a head of a family among the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel after the fall of Jerusalem. His descendants are listed in the register of repatriates (Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59), which shows that he was a figure significant enough for his lineage to be documented during the return.
H8203M.origine: The name Schephathia means "the Lord has judged," composed of two parts: the idea of judgment and the name of God (Yahweh). This name expresses a confession of faith in divine judgment and reflects the common practice in Israel of giving children theophoric names — names containing the name of God or one of His works.
H8203M.emploi: Schephathia appears twice in the Bible, always in contexts of return from exile: in Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59. These two passages are parallel lists of those who returned from Babylonian captivity with the governor Zerubbabel. In these enumerations, the names are grouped by family, and Schephathia is presented as a clan leader, indicating that he had numerous descendants to form a recognizable unit among the restored people.

sens: Son of Mahalalel and father of Amaria, who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile
H8203N.detail: Schephathia is an ancestor of the family of Judah who returned to live in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. His name means "the Lord has judged." He is mentioned in the genealogy in Nehemiah 11:4 as a link in a chain connecting Perez (a distant ancestor) to Ahitub (one of the inhabitants of Jerusalem upon return). He represents one of the families that rebuilt Jewish life after the exile.
H8203N.origine: The name Schephathia comes from Hebrew and means "God (Yah) has judged" (shaphat = to judge, yah = the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it. Such a name proclaims the faith of the parent who gave it: it is the Lord who judges and decides destiny.
H8203N.emploi: Schephathia appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:4, in a context of genealogical lists drawn up after the return from Babylonian exile. It serves as a historical trace of the reconstruction of Jerusalem: the families of Judah and Benjamin who resettled in the holy city are enumerated. Schephathia is mentioned only by his place in this genealogy, with no personal story reported.

sens: Prince of Judah, son of Mattan, advisor to King Zedekiah
H8203O.detail: Schephathia is a prince of Judah who lived during the time of King Zedekiah, just before the fall of Jerusalem. His name means "The Lord has judged." He is mentioned in Jeremiah 38:1 as one of the four advisors to the king who heard the words of the prophet Jeremiah preaching surrender to Babylon, and who later threw him into a cistern to silence him (Jeremiah 38:6).
H8203O.origine: The name Schephathia is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Shephat" (judged) and "Yah" (the Lord). It thus means "The Lord has judged." It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the name of God, common among the royal and noble families of Israel.
H8203O.emploi: Schephathia appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 38:1, where he is mentioned alongside three other princes of Judah: Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashhur. These four men heard Jeremiah tell the people that they must surrender to Babylon, or the city would be destroyed. Furious at this message which they deemed defeatist, they obtained permission from the king to eliminate the prophet. Schephathia thus represents the hostile opposition of the leaders to the Word of God at the time of final judgment on Judah.
H8203O.portee: The story of Schephathia shows us how powerful men resist the Word that God sends through His prophets, even when it is true and beneficial. These leaders, including Schephathia, preferred illusion to truth, and persecuted Jeremiah instead of listening to him. It serves as a warning: any position, even a high one, is only meaningful if it submits to the will of God.

sens: Character from the Wilderness Period, father of Kemuel
H8204.detail: Schiphtan is an Israelite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Moses organizes the distribution of the promised land among the twelve tribes. He is the father of Kemuel, whom he chose as prince (chief) representing the tribe of Ephraim during this important distribution. His name literally means "the one who judges" or "the judge," which may evoke an important function or quality in his family or tribe.
H8204.origine: The name Schiphtan derives from a Hebrew root meaning "to judge" or "to render justice." It is a theophoric name (bearing a meaning related to governance or judgment) typical of the biblical period. The meaning "the judge" suggests that this family may have been associated with judicial or leadership functions among the Ephraimites.
H8204.emploi: Schiphtan appears only once in the Scriptures, in Numbers 34:24, where he is identified as the father of Kemuel. This passage reports the organization of the distribution of the territory of Canaan by twelve men, one representative from each tribe. Kemuel is designated for the tribe of Ephraim, indicating that Schiphtan was a respected figure from this tribe, whose descendants received a prominent role in this sacred distribution.

sens: High place, mountain or hilltop
Bare and arid land, devoid of vegetation
Exposed and visible place from afar
In religious language, place of idolatrous worship
H8205.detail:
1. The word primarily designates elevated terrain, a hill or a summit: in Numbers 23:3, Balaam goes up to "a high place" to watch for a divine revelation. It is a dominant point in the landscape.

2. These heights are often bare and sterile, devoid of trees or greenery: in Isaiah 41:18, God promises to make rivers flow on the "hills" and springs in the valleys, contrasting with the harsh nature of these arid places. In Isaiah 49:9, the released captives "will find pastures on all the hills."

3. Being bare and dominant, these heights are visible and accessible from afar. In Jeremiah 3:2, the prophet commands: "Lift up your eyes to the heights, and see!" — they attract attention.

4. In the Bible, these elevated places become centers of idolatry: in Jeremiah 3:21 and 4:11, the "high places" are associated with Israel's religious infidelity, where the people bowed down to false gods instead of worshiping the true God.
H8205.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of nudity or exposure: a height is an open terrain, without vegetative cover. The same root can express absence or emptiness. In biblical Hebrew, this word specifically designates the bare hills or summits that punctuate the landscape of the Near East, a striking contrast to the green valleys.
H8205.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the prophets: three times in Jeremiah, twice in Isaiah, and in Numbers and other books. It primarily designates natural relief — places where one can stand, observe, pray, or take refuge. But it quickly takes on a religious charge: starting from Jeremiah, the "heights" become symbols of Israelite idolatry, as it is on these elevated, visible, and accessible places that Israel turned away from the true God to worship idols. This nuance is crucial for understanding the prophetic rebukes.
H8205.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that Israel's sin — idolatry — had privileged and visible places. It invites reflection: where do our "heights" lie? What are the places or moments where we are tempted to turn away from God? The contrast between bare heights and fertile valleys also suggests that the true blessing of God transforms even the most arid lands — a promise of grace.

sens: Character from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Ir
Merarite Levite, gatekeeper of the west gate of the temple under David
H8206G.detail:
1. Schuppim is primarily a man from the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Bela, himself a son of Benjamin. He is the son of Ir and the brother of Huppim and Maaca (1 Chronicles 7:12). His sister Maaca is an important figure, married to Makir.
2. Schuppim also refers to a Levite from the family of Merari, son of Hosah. During the time of King David, he was responsible for guarding the west gate of the temple, a position of trust that shows his role in the organized worship of Israel.
H8206G.origine: The name Schuppim means "snakes" in Hebrew, formed from a root that evokes the idea of crawling or slithering. This name was borne by at least two men in ancient Israel — one in the civil genealogy of Benjamin, the other among the servants of Levitical worship — showing that it was not uncommon in families of that time.
H8206G.emploi: Schuppim appears exactly twice in the Old Testament, both in 1 Chronicles 7, a chapter dedicated to the genealogies of the northern tribes. In 1 Chronicles 7:12, he is listed among the descendants of Benjamin and Bela. In 1 Chronicles 7:15, the genealogical context mentions Schuppim again, this time in relation to Makir who took a wife "from Huppim and Schuppim," likely to designate the families of these two brothers. These two occurrences pertain to genealogical and administrative records: one concerns civil lineage, the other cultic responsibility at the temple.

sens: Levite from the family of Merari, gatekeeper of the temple under the reign of David
H8206H.detail: Schuppim is a Levite from the family of Merari, son of Hosa. He is designated to guard the western gate of the temple, called the gate of Shalleketh, during the time of King David. In 1 Chronicles 26:16, he is mentioned alongside his father Hosa, who himself is in charge of the western side; Schuppim shares this important responsibility of overseeing the entrance to the sanctuary.
H8206H.origine: The name Schuppim literally means "snakes" in Hebrew, although the exact etymology and reason for this name remain unclear. It is characteristic of Hebrew names from the monarchical period to refer to natural images or figures.
H8206H.emploi: Schuppim appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:16. This verse is part of a listing of the porters and guardians of the temple established under David, who organized the liturgical service with great structure and rigor. The context shows that the Levitical porters formed teams responsible for the different gates of the sanctuary, and that this charge was entrusted to men of proven lineage and an established house.

sens: venomous snake characterized by its horns
animal that bites treacherously by surprise
hidden threat that strikes suddenly
H8207.detail:
1. The viper is a venomous snake recognizable by its horns — this is why it is called the "horned viper." It is a real animal from the Middle East, dangerous and feared. In Genesis 49:17, the viper represents the hidden danger on the path.
2. The word evokes treacherous attack: the viper does not announce itself, it hides in the shadows and strikes the rider at the heels when he passes near it. It is the image of one who acts stealthily, without warning.
3. Figuratively, "viper" refers to any hidden threat that suddenly arises to harm or overturn. In Jacob's blessing on Dan, the word paints a character: Dan will be one who strikes by surprise, waiting for the opportunity to bite his enemy when he least expects it.
H8207.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁפִיפֹן is closely related to the image of the hissing and biting snake. The root expresses the idea of a quick and treacherous strike. In Greek, this same animal is rendered by the word "aspis" (a viper). The name reflects the natural reality of the ancient Levant, where this venomous snake was well known and feared.
H8207.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 49:17, in Jacob's prophetic blessing on the tribe of Dan. It is used in the literal sense first — there are indeed vipers on the paths — but it immediately becomes an image of Dan's character: quick, striking by surprise, formidable. This comparison reveals that Dan will be a warrior and fighting tribe, acting with the cunning and speed of the serpent.
H8207.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible borrows images from nature to describe characters and destinies. For the reader, it teaches that cunning can be a form of strength — Dan will not overcome by brute force but by agility and surprise attack. It is also a warning: one who acts treacherously, like a viper, can only expect downfall and judgment.

sens: City of Judah
H8208.detail: Shaphir is a locality in Judah mentioned by the prophet Micah. It appears in a judgment oracle where the prophet lists several cities that will be affected by ruin (Micah 1:11).
H8208.origine: The name Shaphir means "beautiful" or "fair" in Hebrew, derived from a root that evokes beauty and brightness. It is a significant name: ironically, the once beautiful city will be humiliated and brought to shame according to the prophet's word.
H8208.emploi: Shaphir appears only once in the Bible, in Micah 1:11. It is among a series of cities in the southern kingdom of Judah that Micah denounces for their injustice. The prophet uses these names of real places to announce that God's judgment will reach the entire region, sparing no local communities.

sens: Having an appearance pleasing to look at, pleasant to the eye
Distinguished by the brilliance or magnificence of its physical aspect
H8209.detail: 1. The word describes what is pleasing to look at, what attracts the eye by its brilliance or harmony. In the vision of Nebuchadnezzar reported in Daniel, the royal tree has "beautiful" foliage, meaning resplendent and magnificent: this tree produces abundant food, provides shade for the beasts, and shelters the birds (Daniel 4:12). 2. The word can also emphasize the magnificence or splendor of a thing considered as a whole. The tree in the dream is described not only as "beautiful" in foliage but also as bearing abundant fruit, symbolizing its excellence and nourishing power (Daniel 4:21).
H8209.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." It describes the outward appearance that pleases the eye, particularly in plants and material things. In Aramaic of the Septuagint, this word corresponds to notions of visible clarity and magnificence.
H8209.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in the same passage of the book of Daniel (4:12 and 4:21). It qualifies the foliage of a monumental tree in the prophetic vision of the Babylonian king. In this context, the beauty of the tree is not merely aesthetic: it also expresses its power, fertility, and ability to nourish all living beings. The word thus emphasizes that what is truly beautiful is also what is useful, fruitful, and a source of life.
H8209.portee: This word invites the believer to perceive that authentic beauty, according to the Bible, is linked to fruitfulness and the ability to give life. The tree in the dream is beautiful because it nourishes and protects; beauty is not a mere appearance, but the outward expression of a deep reality of strength and blessing. For the disciple, this reminds us that what truly matters is not vain splendor, but the fruitful life one can produce in service to others.

sens: to build an earthwork against a besieged city
to erect military terraces and fortifications to attack or block a stronghold
to raise, to build siege works
H8210I.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to construct a ramp or earthwork against the walls of a besieged city. This is a military tactic: the besieging army accumulates earth and materials to form a slope that allows them to reach the top of the fortifications and breach them. Jeremiah 6:6 commands: "Cut down the trees, raise up mounds against Jerusalem!" 2. The word is used more broadly for all siege works: to build fortifications, fortified camps, battering rams, around a city that one wants to conquer. Ezekiel 4:2 lists these works: "Build siege works, raise up mounds against it, surround it with a camp, set battering rams against it all around." 3. Figuratively, the verb expresses the action of raising, building, or elevating something, but in the biblical usages provided, it always retains this military and technical character.
H8210I.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁפַךְ (shaphakh) means at its root "to pour, to spill." The meaning of "to build a siege mound" comes from a metaphorical extension: one "pours" or "accumulates" earth to form the terraces. This verb is frequently used in Hebrew to describe military actions and siege works, particularly among the prophets when they describe God's judgments on rebellious cities.
H8210I.emploi: This verb appears about 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in accounts of military sieges and the prophecies of Ezekiel. It is found in the stories of the kings (2 Samuel, 2 Kings), where Joab and the Assyrian armies raise siege works against the cities (2 Samuel 20:15). Ezekiel constantly uses it to symbolize God's judgments: the prophet must act out the siege of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 4:2), and the word of the Lord promises that Pharaoh will not be able to help because siege mounds will be raised (Ezekiel 17:17). The term marks the inexorability of these military judgments.
H8210I.portee: For the reader, this word evokes the destructive power of military siege and, in the prophetic context, the certainty of God's judgment on sin. Ezekiel uses this language of siege to show that Jerusalem cannot flee or escape the consequences of its rebellion: the walls fall, help does not arrive, punishment comes from all sides. It is a call to repentance through the picture of the inevitable.

H8211.fr: place for the deposit of ashes
sens: Place where the ashes from the altar are poured or thrown
Heap or deposit of accumulated ashes
H8211.detail:
1. The word designates the place, outside the camp, where the ashes from the altar of sacrifices were poured. It is a pure location, reserved for this ritual deposit: in Leviticus 4:12, the ashes of the bull burned as a sin offering are taken outside the camp and burned "on the heap of ashes," which is this regular deposit place.
2. The word can also simply refer to the accumulation of ashes itself, the heap that forms over time, rather than the geographical location where it is found.
H8211.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to pour," "to spread" (it is also used for pouring oil or libations). The name retains the idea of action — pouring — to designate the place where ashes are regularly poured. It is a functional naming: this place is called "the place of deposit" because that is where the ashes are poured.
H8211.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 4:12. It is part of the laws of sacrifice for sin: the priest had to take certain remains of the sacrifice outside the camp, to the place of the ashes, in order to burn them there. This ritual detail emphasizes that the ashes of the sacrifices did not remain in the holy place but were orderly removed to a pure and separate location.
H8211.portee: This passage shows the importance of order and purity in Israelite worship: even the ashes of sacrifices, which addressed sin, had to be treated with care and removed ritually. This reflects the holiness of God and the necessity of a clear separation between the unclean and the clean, a lesson that Christians can meditate on when considering the purification that Christ brings.

sens: Canal through which urine flows in men
By extension, the male genital organ itself
H8212.detail:
1. The urethra is the anatomical canal through which urine flows from the body in men. The Hebrew word emphasizes this function of passage, of conduit: it is formed from a root that evokes the flow or effusion of liquid. In Deuteronomy 23:1, the law lists cases of infirmities that prohibit entry into the assembly of the people: one whose urethra has been cut is excluded, just like one whose testicles have been crushed or removed.
2. The word can also refer more broadly to the male genital organ of which this canal is a part. It is a medical and anatomical term, without pejorative connotation in the Bible: it simply names the reality of the body created by God.
H8212.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to pour," "to spread," "to flow." The urethra is designated by its primary function: it is the conduit through which liquids flow. This image of passage and effusion illuminates the meaning of the word in its legal and ritual context.
H8212.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 23:1. It is included in a list of physical conditions that rendered a man unfit to participate in the religious assemblies of Israel. The law precisely enumerates: one who has crushed or removed testicles, one whose genital organ has been mutilated. This prescription reflected the importance that Mosaic law attached to physical integrity and reproductive capacity in the communal and cultic life of the people.
H8212.portee: This verse invites the Christian reader to meditate on the dignity of the human body in creation, and on how the Law protected the physical wholeness of each individual. Although Christians are no longer bound by these ceremonial rules, the passage reminds us that God knows and respects the realities of the body. It is also an opportunity to recognize how Jesus abolished these ritual separations: in Christ, no one is excluded from communion with God because of their body.

sens: To become low, to sink down
To be humiliated, to lose one's honor or importance
To reduce someone to powerlessness or to submit them
To flatten, to level, to destroy what was elevated
H8213.detail:
1. To become low, to sink down: this is primarily the physical movement of descending or sinking. In Isaiah 40:4, valleys are raised and mountains are lowered, as in a leveling of the terrain.
2. To be humiliated, to lose one's honor or importance: when a person lowers themselves, they acknowledge their weakness or guilt. In Psalms 18:28, God lowers the haughty looks of those who defiantly challenge Him with pride.
3. To reduce someone to powerlessness or to submit them: to lower is to bring someone down from their position of strength. In 1 Samuel 2:7, the Lord lowers those who rise up to show that no power escapes Him.
4. To flatten, to level, to destroy what was elevated: the word also denotes the destruction of fortifications or castles. In Isaiah 25:12, the high walls of the enemy city are lowered and reduced to dust.
H8213.origine: The verb שׁפל comes from a root that expresses the idea of slope, descent, or lowness. The simple form (Qal) describes the state of something or someone becoming low; the intensive form (Hiphil) expresses the active action of lowering, reducing. This family is found in the word שׁפל itself which means "low," "humble," reflecting the image of one who bends down.
H8213.emploi: The verb appears 29 times in the Old Testament, notably in the Psalms and in Isaiah, where it describes God's sovereign action over the powerful. In 1 Samuel 2:7, God lowers and raises according to His will. The Psalms often use it to speak of the humiliation of the proud and the disdain of haughty looks (Psalms 18:28). In Proverbs, the word recurs to show that humility is better than pride (Proverbs 16:19, 29:23). In Isaiah, it describes the destruction of human powers that oppose God: fortifications are lowered, the looks of the haughty are brought down. The context reveals that this lowering is always a divine work, a judgment or correction.
H8213.portee: This word teaches that God alone controls human destinies: no one can remain high when He lowers them, and no one remains low when He raises them. It invites the believer not to fear temporal lowering, for God can honor those He has humbled. It also calls for vigilance against pride, which attracts lowering: "Whoever exalts themselves will be humbled, and whoever humbles themselves will be exalted" is a spiritual law that this word constantly illustrates.

sens: To reduce someone or something to a lower or humble position
To humiliate someone by depriving them of their greatness or power
To break someone's pride by bringing them down
H8214.detail: 1. The verb expresses the action of making something descend, reducing it to a low position: it is a concrete act of lowering. In Daniel 4:37, God can "lower those who walk with pride" — He reduces them to nothing despite their arrogance. 2. It also means to humiliate someone, taking away the greatness they had given themselves. In Daniel 5:19, King Nebuchadnezzar "lowered those he wished," depriving them of their power and honor. 3. The word sometimes designates the very attitude of one who accepts their lowering: "you did not humble your heart" (Daniel 5:22) means "you did not recognize your smallness before God." It is a heart that refuses to bow.
H8214.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of becoming low, of descending. It belongs to a family of words where the contrast between the elevated and the low, between pride and humility, is found. The form used here (Aphel) adds the idea that someone makes another person descend: it is not just being low, it is being lowered.
H8214.emploi: The verb appears only four times in the Greek New Testament, all in Daniel, a prophetic book rich in visions. It is used to describe God's action of humbling the proud (Daniel 4:37), that of the king who controls destinies (Daniel 5:19 and 7:24), and the attitude of the heart in the face of its own fall (Daniel 5:22). Lowering is always linked to the theme of pride and justice: God or sovereign power lowers one who has elevated themselves without right.
H8214.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of a fundamental truth: pride precedes a fall, and only God can truly lower or elevate according to His justice. One who refuses to "humble their heart" before the Lord exposes themselves to divine judgment. In contrast, authentic humility — accepting to recognize one's smallness — is the door that opens to God's grace.

sens: Of lower condition or rank, without prestige or authority
Humble, devoid of grandeur or dignity
H8215.detail:
1. The word designates a person of low rank, without status or honor — one who would be looked down upon. In Daniel 4:17, Nebuchadnezzar learns that God can elevate "the most vile of men" to royal power: even the most despised, the most forgotten man can become great if it pleases the Most High. This is an image of humiliation and social insignificance.
2. The word can also qualify a humble or unworthy condition: lacking grandeur, prestige, being without glory. This humility is not a moral virtue, but a state of fact — one who has nothing, who counts for no one in the eyes of the world.
H8215.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to lower, to humiliate" (in Hebrew שָׁפֵל). The Aramaic form שְׁפַל draws from this same root: the central idea is one of lowering, either physically (to remain low) or socially (to lose dignity and prestige). It is the opposite of exaltation or honor.
H8215.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:17. It is used to express the dramatic contrast between the deepest human humility and the omnipotence of God: even the man judged to be the most vile, the most unworthy by the world's standards, can be elevated by the Most High. The context is that of Nebuchadnezzar's dream and the lesson God wants to teach him about his own reign — a lesson on the relativity of human greatness.
H8215.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not judge according to appearances or human prestige. Low condition, poverty, or obscurity are never a limit for God: He elevates whom He wills, despite the world's disdain. For the Christian, it is a comforting promise: your dignity does not depend on your social status, and God can lift you from the deepest humiliation.

sens: State of poverty or material misery
Condition of humiliation or social dishonor
Situation of weakness or dependence in the face of someone more powerful
H8216.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes poverty, lack of resources, and material precariousness — this state of deprivation felt as oppression. Psalms 136:23 speaks of the people of Israel "humiliated" (or brought low) in the slavery of Egypt, reduced to servitude and destitution. 2. Beyond the lack of goods, the word also evokes shame, loss of dignity — the humiliation one suffers when despised or mistreated. It is the opposite of prestige and honor. 3. More broadly, it designates any condition of weakness, subjugation, or low social rank. Ecclesiastes 10:6 illustrates this in contrast: wealthy and high-ranking men fall into "humiliation," while fools rise to high positions — an inversion that shows how fortune can shift.
H8216.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of being low, being down, descending. It is related to images of physical depression, loss of status, or degradation. The root expresses the opposite of elevation: one moves from high to low, one falls, one is brought low. It is a word that paints the state, not the action of descending.
H8216.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In the Psalms, it describes the oppression of Israel in Egypt — a situation where the entire people was reduced to slavery and misery. In Ecclesiastes, it illustrates the reversals of fortune: the rich who enjoyed wealth and prestige suddenly find themselves impoverished, dishonored, humiliated. Both usages show a lasting state of decline, material or social, that weighs on those who endure it.
H8216.portee: This word reminds us that humiliation and poverty are realities that God does not ignore: He "remembered" the humiliated Israel and freed them. It also invites reflection on the reversals of life: human wealth and honors are unstable, and only God establishes true order. For the believer, recognizing humiliation — one's own or that of others — is turning towards divine mercy.

sens: Located at a lower level
Occupying a position of little importance or weakness
Who is lowered, degraded in honor
Characterized by humility, modesty
H8217.detail:
1. The literal sense describes what is physically low or depressed: in Leviticus 13:20, the leprous spot that appears "depressed" in the skin, sunk below the surface level, is a sign of impurity.
2. It also denotes a low social condition, a humble or despised position: in 2 Samuel 6:22, David says he wants to show himself "vile" and "lower" publicly, accepting a low rank in the eyes of others.
3. The word evokes humiliation, the state of a person brought low, stripped of their honor: Ezekiel 17:14 speaks of the kingdom "held in humiliation," unable to rise again.
4. Finally, it characterizes the humble attitude, the contrite spirit: Psalms 138:6 says that God sees the "humble" and recognizes those whose hearts are small, devoid of pride.
H8217.origine: The Hebrew root שׁפל (shaphal) expresses the fundamental idea of what is low, brought low, in contrast to what is high. It is related to the concept of descending or causing to descend. This word opposes everywhere in the Bible to "high" (gaboah): God is high and remains above, while the humble man is low. Biblical humility is not primarily a moral virtue, but a rightly recognized position before God.
H8217.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mostly in the poetic and prophetic books. In the context of the Law (Leviticus), it describes the physical aspect of a skin lesion. In 2 Samuel and the Psalms, it denotes the humility of heart or voluntary lowering before God. In the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Malachi), it speaks of the humiliation of nations and the renewal of humbled hearts. The word can also apply to the lowering of a kingdom or power: Ezekiel repeats that the "lowered" tree will be raised according to divine purpose. Everywhere, it expresses either an objective inferiority or a spiritual virtue.
H8217.portee: This word teaches that humility is not a weakness, but the right posture of the believer before God. One who accepts to be low, who renounces their own honor, receives God's gaze and His help. Conversely, pride (raised, exalted) opposes God's action. For the Christian, this means that true greatness begins with the acceptance of our smallness before the Most High, as David understood.

sens: State of being lowered, brought low
Humiliation, moral or social degradation
Low place, depression of the ground
H8218.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action or physical state of being lowered, pushed down. In Isaiah 32:19, the city is "deeply lowered" by hail: it is literally thrown to the ground, reduced to the lowest level.
2. By extension, it expresses humiliation — the lowering of one who loses their honor, rank, or dignity. It is a moral and social fall, not just physical.
3. The word can also simply designate a low place, a depression of the ground, the spot where one descends.
H8218.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root שׁפל (shéfal), which means "to be low, to descend." It evokes the simple image of what lowers toward the ground. The root is very ancient and appears in several Hebrew words related to lowness, depth, and degradation.
H8218.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 32:19. It is used there to describe the destruction of a city by hail: the city, struck from heaven, is "deeply lowered," plunged into ruin and humiliation. The poetic context of the prophet Isaiah emphasizes the contrast between divine judgment and the promises of salvation that precede it.
H8218.portee: This word reminds us that lowering — whether physical or moral — does not escape God's sovereignty. In a context of prophetic judgment, it shows how God can humiliate the powers that oppose Him. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize that true dignity comes not from the position we occupy, but from our submission to God.

sens: region of low hills between the Judean mountains and the Mediterranean coast
fertile area suitable for agriculture and livestock
strip of territory conquered or controlled by Israel
H8219.detail:
1. The Shephelah is the region of rolling hills located west of the Judean mountains, forming a transition between the highlands and the coastal plain. It stretches from north to south, particularly in Judea. In Joshua 10:40, we learn that Joshua "defeated all the country, the hill country, the Negev, and the Shephelah," presenting it as a distinct geographical area alongside other regions of Israel.
2. It is a fertile and productive area, particularly favorable for crops and livestock. The texts show intensive agricultural activities: thus in 1 Chronicles 27:28 and 2 Chronicles 26:10, we see shepherds and vine growers established in the Shephelah, testifying to its agricultural wealth.
3. For Israel, possessing the Shephelah meant controlling a strategic and prosperous region. When the Philistines invade it in 2 Chronicles 28:18, it is presented as a major defeat; when Jeremiah announces the return of the captives, he mentions the Shephelah among the restored regions (Jeremiah 32:44).
H8219.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁפֵלָה (shephelah) comes from the root שׁפַל (shapal), which means "to be low" or "to humble oneself." The name literally describes a "low region" in contrast to the mountains that dominate it. It is a technical geographical term used in the Old Testament to designate this specific area between the Judean mountain range and the coastal plain. No major family word stands out in biblical usages.
H8219.emploi: The Shephelah appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Kings, Chronicles) and among the prophets (Jeremiah, Obadiah, Zechariah). It is mentioned in descriptions of conquests and the division of territory after the arrival in Canaan (Joshua 9:1; 11:2, 16; 15:33). The term also appears when listing the regions of Israel (Deuteronomy 1:7; Joshua 10:40; 12:8), showing that it is a natural and administrative division of the land. The kings of Judah develop agricultural resources and livestock there (1 Kings 10:27; 2 Chronicles 1:15; 9:27). Its fortifications and inhabitants play a role in wars and relations with the enemy: Judges 1:9; 2 Chronicles 28:18; Jeremiah 17:26; Obadiah 1:19.
H8219.portee: The Shephelah reminds us that the possession of the land of Canaan was not a passive gift, but included diverse regions, each with its challenges. This geographical name anchors the history of Israel in a concrete and visible reality: an area that the readers of the time saw and traversed. It also symbolizes that God's blessing was expressed in the fertility and material prosperity of the people established on their territory.

sens: State of one who does not work, who remains inactive
Laziness, sluggishness in action
Negligence, letting go in the maintenance of what belongs to us
H8220.detail:
1. Idleness primarily refers to inactivity, the state of doing nothing, remaining without occupation. It is the opposite of work and effort. In Ecclesiastes 10:18, it appears as the cause of a house's decay: "Through laziness, the rafters sag; through idle hands, the house leaks."
2. The word also encompasses laziness, this tendency to flee from effort and prefer inaction to labor. It is a disposition of the heart that refuses to engage in work.
3. Idleness concretely leads to negligence: one who does not act allows what they should care for to deteriorate. The house that collapses in Ecclesiastes 10:18 shows how inaction destroys what work builds and maintains.
H8220.origine: The Hebrew word shiph'lout comes from a root that evokes the idea of sagging, becoming weak or soft. It is related to words meaning "low," "humble," "depression": idleness lowers a person and degrades them morally and materially. It is a poetic and wise term, very appropriate to the book of Ecclesiastes, which meditates on the meaning of life and the consequences of our choices.
H8220.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 10:18. It is found in a passage where the Preacher enumerates small causes that produce great effects: a little laziness is enough to ruin a house, a little negligence to destroy what has cost effort. The context shows that idleness is not a simple rest, but a form of active negligence that allows what is left unattended to rot and collapse.
H8220.portee: This word reminds the reader that our daily choices — to work or to let go, to act or to remain passive — have real and visible consequences on our life, our home, our responsibilities. Idleness is not innocent: it destroys. For the Christian, it is an invitation to vigilance, order, and to honor work as a legitimate and important part of existence according to God's plan.

sens: Locality or region in the northeast of Canaan, on the eastern border
H8221.detail: Shepham is a place or region located in the northeast of Canaan, marking the eastern boundary of the territory of Israel. It appears in the description of the borders that God commands Moses to delineate for the Promised Land: it serves as a landmark between Hazar-enan and Riblah, delineating the territory to the east and towards the Sea of Kinnereth (Numbers 34:10-11). The name suggests a bald or bare place.
H8221.origine: The Hebrew name means "bald" or "bare," perhaps referring to the appearance of the terrain or the nature of the landscape in this region of northeast Canaan.
H8221.emploi: Shepham is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in the context of Numbers 34 where God specifies to Moses the exact geography of the borders of the Promised Land. It appears as a delimiting point in the outline of the eastern boundary of the territory, between Hazar-enan to the north and Riblah to the south, playing a purely geographical role in this territorial delineation.

sens: The hair that grows on a man's chin and cheeks
Mark of dignity and personal honor
Sign of mourning or shame when covered
H8222.detail:
1. The beard is the collection of hair that covers the lower part of a man's face. In Leviticus 13:45, the leper must cover his beard as a sign of his ritual impurity, showing that what is visible on the face is affected by the disease.
2. For a respectable man, a well-groomed beard expresses dignity and social status. When Mephibosheth "had not cared for his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes" (2 Samuel 19:24), this neglect reveals his affliction and distress during the king's absence.
3. Covering the beard is a gesture of mourning, shame, or confusion in the face of a disaster. Ezekiel is commanded not to cover his beard (Ezekiel 24:17), which is an extraordinary prophetic sign of judgment without mourning. Micah describes the false prophets who "will cover their beard" in confusion, as God will not answer them (Micah 3:7).
H8222.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂפָם comes from a root that designates facial hair. The beard was very important in Hebrew culture as a mark of masculinity and male maturity. A man without a beard or with a neglected beard was considered humiliated or in distress.
H8222.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, always in connection with mourning, ritual purity, or personal dignity. In Leviticus, it marks the impurity of the leper. In 2 Samuel, neglecting one's beard expresses prolonged mourning and affliction. In the passages from Ezekiel, covering the beard is the classic gesture of mourning or shame. Micah uses it to describe the confusion of false prophets in the absence of divine response. The beard thus always carries a moral or ritual significance, never purely cosmetic.
H8222.portee: The beard in the Bible symbolizes more than physical appearance: it represents dignity, status, and integrity of man. Its neglect or covering speaks of suffering, mourning, or humiliation. This reminds the reader that the visible body expresses the state of the soul and that our outward presentation reflects what we experience internally.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H8223.detail: Schapham is a leader of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the Bible, during the census of the families of Gad who lived in Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:12). He is listed as second in the hierarchical order, after Joel and before Jaenaï and Schaphath, suggesting that he held recognized authority among the clans of his tribe.
H8223.origine: The name Schapham means "bold" or "fearless" in Hebrew, reflecting the character or reputation of the leader. This type of name reflects the warrior values of the desert tribes and Bashan, a region known for being a challenging territory.
H8223.emploi: Schapham appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:12, in the genealogical list of the leaders of Gad during the divided monarchy. These genealogical lists preserve the memory of the great families and figures of authority among God's people, even though we have no other detailed account about him.

sens: Location in the Negev in southern Judah
H8224.detail: Siphmoth is a small town in southern Judah, in the Negev region. Its Hebrew name evokes the idea of fertility or abundance. It appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 30:28, when King David, after a victory against the Amalekites, distributes plunder to various towns in Judah that had supported him, including those of Siphmoth.
H8224.origine: The Hebrew name Siphmoth literally means "fruits" or "harvests" (from the root that speaks of harvest and abundance). It is a typical place name from southern Palestine, likely reflecting the relative fertility of this region or the hopes that the inhabitants placed in it. The exact site has not been definitively identified by modern archaeology.
H8224.emploi: Siphmoth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 30:28. It is in the context where David, having become king and recognized as the protector of the southern towns of Judah, shares with them the plunder he took from the Amalekites. This mention shows that Siphmoth was a recognized locality in the Negev, significant enough to be listed among the beneficiaries of his royal generosity.

sens: Person from a locality called Schepham or Siphmoth
H8225.detail: Shimei, designated as being from Schepham, is named in the list of King David's officials responsible for royal stewardship. His nickname indicates that he came from a locality called Schepham or Siphmoth (1 Chronicles 27:27). He is a trusted man assigned to oversee the storage of wine provisions in the vineyards, an important role for the royal economy.
H8225.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁפְמִי (shiph.mi) is a demonym, meaning a term that designates someone according to their geographical origin. It derives from the place name Schepham or Siphmoth, the exact meaning of which remains uncertain. The formation with the suffix -mi is typical in Hebrew for forming adjectives or names of peoples from place names.
H8225.emploi: Schepham appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:27, in the enumeration of the twelve officials responsible for King David's goods. Shimei from Schepham oversees the reserves of wine stored in the vineyards, a position of major economic responsibility at the royal palace. This historical mention is part of the record of officials and administrators of the kingdom under David's reign.

sens: That which is buried, hidden in the earth or sand, carefully guarded
That which is accumulated, set aside with care
That which has value and is protected by being concealed
H8226.detail: 1. The word primarily evokes the idea of what is buried or hidden to be preserved: in Deuteronomy 33:19, it literally refers to the hidden riches in the sand of the shores, which the merchants of Sidon will seek. 2. More broadly, it refers to what one accumulates, what one treasures — it is set aside carefully. 3. By extension, it is anything of value because it has been hidden, protected, and jealously guarded: the treasure is precious precisely because it is rare, buried, and difficult to access.
H8226.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of covering, of concealing — as one covers something with earth or sand to hide and protect it. Hence comes the meaning of "treasure": that which is covered, concealed, set aside. The basic image is that of buried treasure, kept secret.
H8226.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in the sense of treasure. Deuteronomy 33:19 places it in Moses' blessing on the tribes of Israel: it speaks of maritime riches — pearls, purple, goods — that Sidon will seek hidden in the sand and in the water. It is a context of commerce, of natural wealth that peoples covet and set aside.
H8226.portee: This passage reminds us that the resources God has hidden in His creation — even under the seas and in the sand — are valuable and intended for the peoples. It invites the reader to recognize the riches and blessings that God has scattered throughout the world, often hidden, waiting to be discovered and appreciated at their true worth.

sens: Small herbivorous mammal resembling a rodent, with short legs and rounded ears
Creature that ruminates but does not have split hooves, classified among unclean animals according to the Law
Animal living in rocks and mountains, known for its group life and vigilance
H8227A.detail:
1. The daman is a small herbivorous animal with a stocky body, short legs, and rounded ears, measuring about 50 centimeters. It is a rodent that lives in rocky regions of the Middle East and Africa. Although it ruminates like ruminants (notably sheep and goats), it does not have split hooves, which distinguishes it from the clean animals permitted for the people of Israel.
2. According to the Law of Moses (Leviticus 11:5 and Deuteronomy 14:7), the daman is among the unclean animals that the Israelites were not to eat. This prohibition is based on a simple rule: a clean animal must both ruminate AND have split hooves. The daman meets the first criterion but fails the second, hence its uncleanness.
3. The daman inhabits mountains and rocky cliffs where it finds refuge and food. Psalm 104:18 describes it finding its home in the rocks, while Proverbs 30:26 praises its collective wisdom: the damans, despite their individual weakness, live in close-knit groups in the rocks, allowing them to survive through mutual aid and vigilance.
H8227A.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁפָן (shaphan) specifically designates the daman or hyrax. This term, attested four times in the Hebrew Bible, reflects careful observation of the animal by the ancient Israelites who shared its territory. The daman was well known to the peoples of the ancient Levant. The French Segond uses the word "daman," borrowed from Arabic and North African languages, to name this characteristic animal of arid regions.
H8227A.emploi: The word shaphan appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in legislative or poetic contexts. Two occurrences are found in the dietary law (Leviticus 11:5 and Deuteronomy 14:7), where the daman is listed among the animals forbidden for Israelite consumption. Two other appearances are in Psalms and Proverbs (Psalms 104:18 and Proverbs 30:26), where the daman becomes an example of wisdom and adaptation to the rocky environment: its peaceful life in the mountains and its fraternity in the group illustrate God's providence and the survival strategy through unity. The context thus shifts from legal to sapiential, from prescriptive to poetic.
H8227A.portee: The daman reminds the reader that the Law divides the created world into categories — clean and unclean — and that this distinction is not arbitrary but based on clear observable criteria. For the believer, this teaches that God orders creation with intention. More profoundly, the daman in Proverbs and Psalms becomes a symbol of humble wisdom: a creature without individual strength that survives through collective intelligence and trust in its rocky refuge, inviting the believer to seek refuge in God rather than in their own strength.

sens: Secretary of King Josiah of Judah
Influential man at court and servant of God during the religious reform
Father of Ahikam, protector of the prophet Jeremiah
H8227B.detail:
1. Schaphan is primarily known as the secretary of King Josiah in the seventh century B.C. He is the one whom the king sends to oversee the repairs of the temple, and he reports to the king the discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple (2 Kings 22:3, 10; 2 Chronicles 34:16). A royal secretary was a powerful figure, responsible for conveying the king's orders and managing the affairs of the kingdom.
2. Schaphan demonstrates faithfulness to God and His work. Upon discovering the Book of the Law, he informs the king, which leads to the great religious reform during Josiah's reign. His actions help restore true worship of the Lord (2 Chronicles 34:16, 18).
3. Schaphan is the father of Ahikam, who himself becomes a significant figure. After the fall of Jerusalem, Ahikam protects the prophet Jeremiah from those who wanted to kill him (Jeremiah 26:24). The protection that Schaphan and his household provide to Jeremiah shows their dedication to the word of God even in the worst circumstances.
H8227B.origine: The name Schaphan literally means "hyrax" or "rock badger" (small rock-dwelling animals mentioned in the Bible). This animal nickname was common in Hebrew onomastics. Schaphan's family left a mark on the religious and political life of Judah: his descendants are mentioned in the book of Jeremiah, including Gemariah and Micaiah, who also heard the word of the Lord.
H8227B.emploi: Schaphan appears 23 times in the Old Testament, primarily in 2 Kings 22, 2 Chronicles 34, and the book of Jeremiah. In 2 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 34, he plays a central role in the discovery and transmission of the Book of the Law to King Josiah. In the book of Jeremiah, his name and that of his family recur to mark the support that Schaphan's household gives to the prophet and his mission: his son Ahikam prevents Jeremiah from being handed over to death (Jeremiah 26:24), and other members of his family listen to the word of God (Jeremiah 36:11). After the exile, Schaphan is still mentioned as an ancestor of Gedaliah, governor of Judah appointed by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:22).
H8227B.portee: Schaphan and his family embody a faithfulness that endures through trials. Although he lived in a time of political and spiritual turmoil, Schaphan remains a servant of God and passes this faithfulness on to his sons. His example shows how a family rooted in obedience to God can exert a beneficial influence, even in times of crisis, and protect the prophets of the Lord. For the Christian reader, Schaphan reminds us of the importance of placing public responsibilities in the service of divine truth.

sens: Father of Jaazaniah, one of the elders of Israel during the time of Ezekiel
H8227G.detail: Schaphan is a proper name referring to a man whose son Jaazaniah is mentioned in a prophetic vision. Ezekiel 8:11 shows him as the father of an elder of Israel who participated in idolatrous acts in the temple, with a censer in hand among seventy other elders.
H8227G.origine: The Hebrew name שָׁפָן literally means "hyrax" or "rabbit-like animal" (a mountain-dwelling animal of the Near East). Like many biblical names, it derives from this animal imagery, though we do not know precisely why this nickname was given to this man.
H8227G.emploi: Schaphan appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 8:11, where he is identified as the father of Jaazaniah. The latter is presented among the seventy elders of the house of Israel who stood before idols and burned incense before them in a vision of the profaned temple. It is possible that this Schaphan is the same character as the secretary of King Josiah mentioned in other books of the Old Testament, but the biblical text itself does not specify this.

sens: wealth, profusion of goods or resources
that which overflows, that which gushes forth in large quantities
H8228.detail:
1. The word denotes a profusion, a material wealth in large quantities. In Deuteronomy 33:19, Moses blesses the tribe of Zebulun by speaking of the "abundance" that the Israelites will draw from the sea — the fishing and commercial riches that will flow from this maritime trade. It is an image of overflowing fertility and prosperity.
2. The underlying image is that of a source that pours forth, a flow that runs generously. The word evokes less a static reserve than a generosity that naturally spills over, like the sea that continually offers its treasures to those who know how to draw from them.
H8228.origine: The Hebrew word שֶׁ֫פַע (shépha') comes from a root that expresses the idea of pouring, gushing forth, overflowing. It literally denotes that which flows or overflows, hence the meaning of abundance. This root evokes an image of natural and continuous generosity, a wealth that does not deplete but flows from a source.
H8228.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Moses' blessing on the tribes (Deuteronomy 33:19). Zebulun is a coastal tribe, devoted to maritime trade and fishing; Moses promises that this tribe will "suck the abundance of the sea," meaning it will enjoy the riches that trade and fishing will provide. The context shows that abundance is the fruit of blessed human activity, not passivity, but an overabundance resulting from work and geographical position.
H8228.portee: This word reminds us that God is the source of prosperity; He promises not a life of idleness, but a generosity overflowing attached to honest activity and work. For the believer, it is an invitation to see that divine blessing can manifest in legitimate material abundance when it is linked to justice and trust in God.

sens: Large group of people moving together
Large quantity of water or liquid flowing
Multitude of animals
Impressive crowd
H8229.detail:
1. An assembly of people moving together: the watchman sees the "troop" of Jehu approaching (2 Kings 9:17), meaning a group of horsemen forming a visible unit from afar.
2. A flow or abundant current, often of water: Job asks if God can make the "torrents" of water rise to the clouds (Job 38:34), an image of water rushing down in quantity.
3. A multitude of gathered animals: Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem covered with a "crowd" of camels coming from distant lands (Isaiah 60:6).
4. An impressive multitude that covers and overwhelms: the enemy horses cover the city with their "multitude," creating a cloud of dust (Ezekiel 26:10).
H8229.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to flow," "to pour out." The basic image is that of a flow or influx: like water that flows abundantly, the troop is that which spills over, pours out in large numbers. The word thus denotes profusion, abundance in the form of movement and mass.
H8229.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament. It is first used for a military troop or a caravan of travelers moving together (2 Kings 9:17). It also describes natural phenomena: waters flowing abundantly (Job 38:34), or animals in great numbers (Isaiah 60:6). Ezekiel uses it to evoke the overwhelming power of an enemy army (Ezekiel 26:10). The common meaning is always a visible and impressive abundance, whether human, animal, or liquid.
H8229.portee: This word helps the reader understand how the Bible speaks of power: not through abstract numbers, but through the concrete image of a crowd that overwhelms, of a flow that rushes down. It shows that God sees and masters these masses (Job 38:34), and that the true wealth of Jerusalem is not its walls but the influx of peoples seeking it (Isaiah 60:6).

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H8230.detail: Schipheï is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Allon and the father of Ziza. His name means "abundant" and he lived during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah, during the period when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms.
H8230.origine: The name Schipheï comes from Hebrew and literally means "abundant." He belongs to a family of Simeonites whose genealogies are carefully preserved in the records of Israel.
