H8230.emploi: Schipheï is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:37. He appears in a genealogy of the descendants of Simeon, presented as a lineage of notable Simeonites. His name is inserted into a genealogical chain: he is the son of Allon and the father of Ziza, which situates his life during the divided monarchy, at the time of King Hezekiah.

sens: to have brightness, to shine
to please by appearance
to be suitable, acceptable
H8231.detail:
1. The word primarily describes visible beauty that shines and attracts the eye — the luster of something well-polished or finely finished. It is the sense of "glisten": something that radiates due to its quality or well-kept appearance.
2. Figuratively, it expresses what pleases, what is beautiful to look at or to possess. In Psalms 16:6, the psalmist says that his inheritance is "beautiful" — not primarily for its price, but because he finds it good, pleasant, suitable in his eyes.
3. More broadly, the word means to be acceptable, suitable, worthy of approval — a notion that extends to anything that deserves to be regarded as good, just, and appropriate.
H8231.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁפַר (shaphar) comes from a root meaning to polish, to make smooth and shiny. In Aramaic, the form שְׁפַר (shepar) carries the same meaning and that of "to be acceptable." The initial image is that of light shining on a polished surface, from which the idea extends to all beauty, all suitability, everything that pleases.
H8231.emploi: The verb appears once in the Hebrew Bible in Psalms 16:6. The context shows a man declaring that the inheritance God has given him — not great wealth, but a fair and suitable lot — is "beautiful" in his eyes. It is a word that values not external magnificence, but what is appropriate, worthy, good to receive. The psalmist expresses his satisfaction and contentment: what has fallen to him is beautiful in his eyes because it comes from God and he recognizes it as just.
H8231.portee: This word teaches that true beauty is not primarily a matter of luxury or striking appearance, but of acceptability and suitability. For the believer, being satisfied with the inheritance that God gives — whether small or large — is to recognize that it is beautiful because it is just. It invites looking beyond appearances and appreciating what comes from God as good and appropriate.

sens: to appear just, suitable, appropriate to the one perceiving it
to please, to be agreeable to someone
to be acceptable or satisfying in a given context
H8232.detail:
1. The word describes what seems just or suitable in someone's eyes. It is the impression of rectitude or appropriateness that something produces. In Daniel 4:2, King Nebuchadnezzar says it seemed good to him — that is, he judged it appropriate and just — to make known the signs and wonders of God.
2. The word also expresses what pleases, what is agreeable or attractive to a person. In Daniel 4:27, the prophet asks the king: may my counsel please you, meaning: may you find it good and welcome it favorably.
3. To be good or acceptable means to correspond to what is expected, to meet a requirement. In Daniel 6:1, Darius found it good to appoint one hundred twenty satraps: this plan seemed appropriate and acceptable to govern his kingdom.
H8232.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that evokes the idea of what shines, what is pure or of good appearance — the image is that of what pleases the eye and the mind. In the biblical Aramaic context, the word describes personal judgment: what seems good or acceptable to the one who decides. It is always an act of will or perception on the part of the one who estimates something.
H8232.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears three times in the book of Daniel, all in contexts of royal decision-making. It expresses the judgment a king makes about a project or counsel. In Daniel 4:2, Nebuchadnezzar judges it good to publish the wonders of God. In Daniel 4:27, Daniel's counsel must please the king for him to change. In Daniel 6:1, Darius finds the administrative plan appropriate. The word reveals how power is decided: by what seems good to the one in command.
H8232.portee: This word invites reflection on the foundation of our judgments. What seems good to us? On what criteria do we decide? The Bible shows that even the most powerful kings decide based on what appears good to them — and often this appearance is deceptive. For the believer, it is about not relying on one's own judgment, but seeking the wisdom of God, who alone knows the true good.

sens: Beauty, grace, splendor of a form
Excellence, nobility of speech
Moral or spiritual perfection
H8233.detail:
1. The word primarily designates visible beauty, the pleasant luster of a form or person — that which delights the eye. In Genesis 49:21, Jacob blesses Naphtali by saying he is "a doe set free" who "utters beautiful words": the image is that of a graceful and elegant creature whose speech breathes nobility.
2. By extension, the word characterizes the excellence and dignity of speech itself, its quality to charm and move. The "beautiful words" of Naphtali are not only pleasing to the ear; they reflect a wisdom and goodness that make them worthy of respect.
3. In a broader sense, beauty evokes perfection, that which is good and worthy of admiration, both materially and morally or spiritually. It is the idea that what is beautiful touches on the divine order.
H8233.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of brightness and splendor. The word belongs to the semantic field of what is convenient, pleasant, excellent — a beauty that pleases and elevates. In the Greek Old Testament, the concept is close to the Greek "kalon" (the beautiful, the good), for in Hebrew and Greek moral beauty and physical beauty are often inseparable.
H8233.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 49:21, where it qualifies the words of Naphtali. Although rare, its usage is precise: it is about praising, in a patriarchal blessing, the grace and nobility of this son of Jacob. The context shows that beauty is not a mere appearance, but a quality that manifests itself through speech and conduct, reflecting the divine grace of which a person or tribe may be endowed.
H8233.portee: This word reminds us that beauty, in the Bible, is never superficial. When Jacob blesses Naphtali by praising his beautiful words, he conveys the idea that grace and excellence of life are divine gifts that reveal themselves in our actions and words. It is an invitation to seek moral beauty — that of the heart and wisdom — rather than mere seduction of appearance.

sens: Desert station visited by the Israelites during the Exodus
H8234.detail: Schapher is the name of a mountain or a stop where the Israelites camped during their journey through the desert, after leaving Egypt. It appears in the list of stations on the journey between Kehélatha and Haradah (Numbers 33:23-24). It is one of the many resting and gathering places of the Hebrew people during their forty years of wandering in the desert.
H8234.origine: The name Schapher means "beauty" in Hebrew. It likely designates a place with remarkable scenery or distinctive geography, located in the Sinai region or the Arabian desert. It is a specific geographical name, with no direct etymological link to other major biblical words.
H8234.emploi: Schapher is mentioned only twice in the Bible, in the itinerary account of Numbers 33, which lists the forty-two stations where Israel camped during the desert. It appears between Kehélatha (v. 23) and Haradah (v. 24), without particular description of the place or special event. This list serves as a memorial of the stages of the divine journey that led the people to the Promised Land.

sens: Clarity, purity of the sky
Serene, radiant aspect
State of calm and peace
H8235.detail:
1. The word denotes the clarity and purity of the sky, that luminous aspect that appears when the clouds dissipate. In Job 26:13, the breath of God gives the sky this serenity: it is the image of a pure and radiant firmament, without veil.
2. By extension, it evokes the serene and radiant aspect of a thing — that effect of calm and clear beauty produced by the order established by God.
3. On a personal or spiritual level, it can also refer to an inner state of peace and tranquility, as the reflection of this celestial clarity in the one who enjoys it.
H8235.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root related to the idea of purity, clarity, and beauty. It paints the image of a clean, clear surface, without stain or darkness. It is both an aesthetic and moral notion: what is pure in the eyes of God is also what shines with radiant clarity.
H8235.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 26:13, where it denotes the clarity that God gives to the sky by His breath. In this magnificent context, where Job's friend enumerates the great works of God — ordering the sky, piercing the fleeing serpent — serenity is one of the marks of His creative power. It is a noble word, used to describe God's major work in the cosmos.
H8235.portee: This word reminds us that God is not only powerful: He is also a God of order, purity, and beauty. The serenity He gives to the sky teaches the believer that behind the storms and troubles of the visible world shines an unshakeable divine clarity. It invites contemplation of the creative majesty and encourages one to seek, by grace, that purity and peace.

sens: Hebrew midwife in ancient Egypt
H8236.detail: Shiphrah is one of the two Hebrew midwives mentioned in the account of oppression in Egypt. Along with her companion Pua, she was ordered by Pharaoh to kill all the boys born to the Hebrews, but she refused to obey this inhumane order and feared God instead of fearing the king (Exodus 1:15-21). Her act of courageous disobedience and protection of the Hebrew children demonstrates faithfulness to God despite the peril.
H8236.origine: The name Shiphrah means "beautiful" or "radiant" in Hebrew, formed from a root evoking beauty or splendor. It reflects a quality of nobility or dignity that stands in stark contrast to the baseness of Pharaoh's order. This personal name is borne by this courageous woman from the time of Moses.
H8236.emploi: Shiphrah appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 1:15, where she is presented as one of the two midwives of the Hebrews in Egypt. The text specifically names her to honor her role in protecting the male newborns. Although the mention is brief, she and Pua symbolize resistance to injustice and the courage to believe in God in the face of an oppressive authority.
H8236.portee: Shiphrah embodies moral courage and the fear of God that takes precedence over the fear of men. Her story encourages the reader to obey conscience and God rather than an unjust order, even at the peril of one's life. It reminds us that God notices and protects those who serve Him faithfully, even in the darkest moments of oppression.

sens: Piece of fabric or cloth intended to cover a surface
Covering spread over a throne or royal place
Symbol of power and domination
H8237.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a fabric, a cloth that is spread to cover something — in this case, the ground or a surface. It is a concrete object of furniture or decoration.
2. In its biblical usage, it takes on a royal and solemn dimension: God tells King Nebuchadnezzar that He will "spread his carpet" over the stones where He has placed His throne (Jeremiah 43:10). The carpet is not just an ornament, but an accessory of possession, the visible mark of the king's power over the place.
3. By extension, the word evokes domination and the installation of power: when a king spreads his carpet, he asserts his sovereignty and authority over that territory.
H8237.origine: The Hebrew word shafrîr has an uncertain etymology; the root and the original image remain debated among scholars. The Segond 1910 translates it as "carpet," suggesting the idea of a spread fabric, but the exact meaning of the Hebrew word in this context remains obscure. This is why ancient lexicons note that "the meaning is doubtful."
H8237.emploi: The word shafrîr appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 43:10. It describes the action of King Nebuchadnezzar who "spreads his carpet" over the stones where God has hidden His throne. This unique and isolated usage makes it difficult to determine the precise meaning: is it a carpet, a canopy, a flag, or another royal adornment? The translation "carpet" is a reasonable conjecture, but it remains cautious.
H8237.portee: This term reminds us that the display of royal power is accompanied by visible and material signs. For the believer, the image of the king who "spreads his carpet" over a land shows how power is displayed and takes possession: it invites us to consider that God's authority is indeed real and visible in history, even when it passes through worldly kings.

sens: the moment immediately before sunrise
the weak and gradual light of morning before day
the beginning of the day, the dawn
H8238.detail:
1. Dawn is that moment very early in the morning, just before the sun rises — when the night begins to pale and the outlines of things become visible again. It is the hour when birds begin to sing and people rise to start their day.
2. The word also denotes the light itself during this period: this soft and growing glow that gradually illuminates the sky and the earth, not yet the full brightness of day, but more than the darkness of night. In Daniel 6:19, King Darius rises "at dawn" to check if Daniel has survived in the lion's den — this indicates the urgency and impatience that drives him: he could not wait for the later morning.
H8238.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁפַרְפָּר (shepharpar) specifically denotes dawn, this daily phenomenon of daybreak. It belongs to the family of words that depict clarity and brightness (like שְׁפַר, "beauty," "splendor"). The underlying image is that of light awakening and growing, gradually driving away the darkness of night.
H8238.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 6:19. In this dramatic account, King Darius, deeply troubled by the placing of his friend Daniel in the lion's den, spends a sleepless night without music. At dawn — that is, at the first light of morning — he rushes to the den to see if Daniel is alive. The choice of this word emphasizes the king's impatience and the critical moment of rescue: he cannot wait any longer; he must know right away. Dawn thus marks here the transition from doubt and nighttime anguish to hope and revelation of the morning.
H8238.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, dawn often symbolizes the moment of revelation, deliverance, and renewed hope. Like the king who discovers at dawn that Daniel is alive, the believer can learn to see each new day as an opportunity to discover God's faithfulness. It is an invitation not to despair in the night, but to wait with confidence for the morning that God brings.

sens: To put an object in a specific location
To establish, found, institute
To entrust, hand over to someone
H8239.detail:
1. To place something: to position a physical object in a given location. In 2 Kings 4:38, Elisha asks his servant to place the large pot on the fire to cook a stew. This is the concrete action of setting something in place.

2. To establish or institute: to give something a solid foundation or stable existence. When Psalm 22:16 speaks of ‘placing’ my feet, it means giving a firm and secure position. This conveys the sense of installing something durably.

3. To hand over to someone, to entrust a task or responsibility. In Isaiah 26:12, God ‘places’ or accomplishes for us all that we do: this suggests the idea of putting something in someone’s hands, giving them charge or the outcome.
H8239.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁפַת (sha-phat) comes from a root that fundamentally expresses the action of putting or installing. The family of the word includes terms related to position or establishment. It is a simple and concrete verb, very common in the Old Testament, describing the basic action of placing something in a location or fixing something in a stable manner.
H8239.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the provided biblical references. In 2 Kings 4:38, it denotes the material action of placing a pot on the fire. In Ezekiel 24:3, the same concrete sense is found with the cauldron. In Isaiah 26:12, the meaning broadens: God ‘places’ or accomplishes our work for us, suggesting the idea of establishing, founding, or bringing to completion. In Psalm 22:16, the verb expresses the action of firming or placing the feet securely. The word thus shifts from the concrete (placing an object) to the figurative (establishing, founding, accomplishing).
H8239.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, God not only creates but also places, establishes, and founds in a lasting way. When God ‘places’ something—our works, our faith, our salvation—it underscores the solidity and certainty of His action. For the believer, this invites us to seek the assurance that God strengthens our steps and brings our works to a good end.

sens: Enclosure or building where livestock is kept
By extension, a place of rest or shelter for animals
H8240A.detail:
1. A stable is a building or enclosure intended to house livestock, particularly cattle. It is a closed space where animals find protection and rest. In Psalms 68:14, the image evokes the flocks resting in their shelter.
2. In a figurative or poetic sense, the word designates any place where creatures find refuge and tranquility. The stable thus symbolizes a place of safety and calm, away from danger and external agitation.
H8240A.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁפַתָּיִם (shaphatayim) likely refers to enclosures or places where livestock gathers. The root carries the idea of a delimitation or a space reserved for animals. In biblical Hebrew, this term belongs to pastoral vocabulary, reflecting the rural and agricultural life of the people of Israel.
H8240A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 68:14. It is found in a poetic image where the psalmist depicts the flocks at rest. The context suggests a peaceful pastoral scene, where the tamed animals (symbolized by the sheep with golden fleece) rest in their enclosures. The rarity of the term and the slight ambiguity of its exact meaning do not diminish its evocative power.
H8240A.portee: This image of a tranquil stable invites the reader to contemplate the peace and security that God offers to His creatures. In the context of Psalm 68, it contributes to the vision of a world ordered by God, where every creature has its place and refuge. For the believer, it is a reminder that God cares even for the humblest and that submission to His will brings peace.

sens: Ledge or cornice of a table or piece of furniture
Protruding edge serving to support or hold something
H8240B.detail:
1. The word designates a projection or cornice—a band that extends—typically on a piece of furniture or surface. In Ezekiel 40:43, it refers to ledges four fingers high arranged around the tables of the temple where the meat of the sacrifices was placed: these ledges helped to delineate the space and prevent the flesh from sliding. It is a concrete and functional architectural element.
2. More broadly, the word can refer to any raised border or cornice serving to support, contain, or delineate. The image is that of a lip or edge marking a boundary.
H8240B.origine: The Hebrew root suggests the idea of a projection or prominence. The word belongs to the vocabulary of architecture and temple furniture. Although the precise etymology is uncertain, it describes a characteristic form: something that extends or borders.
H8240B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 40:43. The context is that of the vision of the future temple that the prophet receives: Ezekiel meticulously describes the architecture of the restored sanctuary, particularly the tables where sacrifices were presented. The ledges of these tables are simple yet important architectural details for the cultic function.
H8240B.portee: This verse shows how the worship of Israel was ordered even in its material details. The ledge of a sacrifice table, though humble, participates in the order and holiness of the temple. For the believer, this reminds us that God is concerned with both grand visions and the small concrete realities of worship service.

sens: Very short moment, quick passage of time
Fleeting flash, sudden and brief manifestation
H8241.detail:
1. This word primarily designates a very short moment, an instant that passes quickly—a fraction of time. In Isaiah 54:8, the prophet speaks of the ‘instant’ when God hid His face: it is only a brief moment compared to the eternity of His compassion.
2. By extension, it evokes a sudden and intense manifestation that lasts little: a flash, a momentary overflow of anger or feeling. This is why this word, related to the Hebrew word for ‘flood,’ retains the idea of something that bursts forth or surges with force, then calms down.
H8241.origine: This word is a variant of the Hebrew term שֶׁטֶף (sheteph), which literally means ‘flood’ or ‘inundation’—an image of sudden and violent overflow. The root thus evokes the rapid movement of water cascading down. Applied to time, it retains this idea of rapid flow, of a moment that flows and passes without stopping.
H8241.emploi: This word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in Isaiah 54:8. It describes an ‘instant’ of anger—a moment when God turns away His face. The context is crucial: this brief instant is contrasted with ‘an eternal love.’ The prophet means to say that divine anger is temporary, while His mercy lasts forever. It is a word of consolation for Israel in exile.
H8241.portee: This verse teaches us that difficult moments, trials, and instances of divine discipline are brief compared to the eternity of His love. For the believer going through suffering, knowing that it is merely an ‘instant’ in the face of the Redeemer's endless compassion becomes a source of hope and trust.

sens: A sack or coarse cloth used to transport or store goods, particularly grains
Rough fabric worn as clothing to express mourning, penitence, or humiliation before God
Gesture and symbol of repentance and divine supplication
H8242.detail:
1. The sack is primarily a practical object: a coarsely woven cloth, often made from goat hair, intended to hold and transport goods such as grains (Genesis 42:25 and 42:35 mention sacks filled with money and wheat). It is an ordinary utensil of the household and commerce.
2. This same rough fabric becomes a garment of distress: it is worn directly on the skin, sometimes by stripping off one's clothes, to manifest one's pain. Jacob tears his clothes and puts on a sack when he believes his son Joseph is dead (Genesis 37:34). It is the quintessential garment of mourning.
3. The sack also symbolizes penitence and supplication: wearing a sack means humbling oneself before God, acknowledging one's sin, or imploring His help. When Hezekiah learns of the Assyrian threat, he covers himself with a sack and goes to the house of the Lord (Isaiah 37:1). The people of Nineveh wear sackcloth as a sign of repentance (Jonah 3:5-8).
H8242.origine: The Hebrew word saq designates this coarse cloth by its very appearance: a rough and thick weave. Its Greek equivalent is sakkos. In Hebrew, it likely comes from a root related to the idea of thick and rough fabric. Throughout the ancient Near East, the sack had this dual function: a container for goods and a symbol of mourning or humiliation, making it an object laden with religious and emotional significance.
H8242.emploi: The word saq appears 47 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical (Samuel, Kings) and prophetic (Isaiah, Jeremiah) books. It designates either the practical object (grain sacks) or the mourning garment. Its use intensifies in contexts of crisis, death, or collective penitence. Hezekiah, David, Job, Esther cover themselves with sackcloth. The prophets command the people to wear sackcloth as a sign of repentance (Jeremiah 4:8, Jeremiah 6:26). The cloth of the sack thus becomes the visible and tangible sign of the inner cry to God: a silent confession of mourning and dependence.
H8242.portee: For the Christian, the sack reminds us that mourning and penitence are not secret feelings: they manifest through concrete actions and visible signs. Wearing sackcloth is to confess before all, before God and before men, that one needs to repent. This ancient practice teaches us that true heart change is often accompanied by a visible change in our behavior and appearance, and that there is no shame in humbling oneself publicly before God.

sens: Part of the human body extending from the hip to the foot
Lower limb that supports the weight of the body and allows one to stand and walk
H8243.detail:
1. The leg is the part of the body between the hip and the foot. In Daniel 2:33, in the vision of the colossal statue seen by Nebuchadnezzar, the legs are made of iron — they represent the strength and solidity of the empire that dominates the known world. This is why iron is chosen: it is the hardest and most robust metal.

2. Figuratively, the leg symbolizes the ability to stand firm, to advance, to walk through life. In this same vision, the iron legs support the rest of the body of the statue, just as military power supports an empire. What is stable on its legs will not fall.
H8243.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוֹק (shoq) literally means the leg, the part of the body that goes from the hip to the foot. It is a simple and concrete word, designating one of the two legs of the body. The Aramaic word שָׁק (shaq) is a direct variant, used in the book of Daniel which is written in Aramaic for several of its chapters. The root evokes the idea of supporting, carrying, as the leg bears the entire weight of the body.
H8243.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Aramaic, in Daniel 2:33, where it refers to the legs of the great statue in Nebuchadnezzar's dream. This prophetic statue represents a succession of empires. The iron legs symbolize the power and dominance of a future empire — likely the Roman Empire according to most interpreters. The choice of iron for the legs emphasizes that this empire rests on exceptional and enduring military strength.
H8243.portee: This vision reminds the reader that earthly powers, even the strongest, are merely fragile creatures compared to God. The iron legs will fall: the statue will be crushed by a stone that becomes a mountain filling the whole earth (Daniel 2:34-35). It is a call not to fear human empires, all of which are destined to disappear, while the kingdom of God remains eternal.

sens: to tie together with a rope or band
to hold a yoke on the neck
to restrain, reduce to servitude
H8244.detail:
1. The verb "to bind" primarily denotes the action of securely tying, of knotting together. In Lamentations 1:14, it is the hand of the Lord that "binds" the yoke of iniquities: the image is that of a yoke attached to the neck of a beast of burden, or of a chained prisoner.
2. But the meaning goes beyond physical binding: "to bind" means to keep someone under a yoke, to subjugate them. The yoke of iniquities, once bound, "intertwined" — the faults accumulate and wrap around like ropes that constrict — and the prophet can no longer flee: it is enslavement.
3. Thus, "to bind" expresses total restraint: it breaks strength ("He has broken my strength"), renders powerless. It reduces someone to the slavery of sin and its consequences.
H8244.origine: The Hebrew verb שׂקַד (saqad) evokes the action of tying, of firmly attaching. It belongs to the lexical field of bonds and restraints. Although rare in the Bible (only one occurrence), it follows the logic of Hebrew verbs of subjugation: a "bound" yoke is a yoke that cannot be removed.
H8244.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Lamentations 1:14. It is a passage of national lamentation where Jerusalem, destroyed, acknowledges that its iniquities — its accumulated faults — have been "bound" upon it like an oppressive yoke. The context is that of divine judgment after the fall of the city. The use of the Niphal (passive form) emphasizes that this bond has been established and maintained: the iniquities are "bound" and cannot be undone.
H8244.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that sin is not merely an isolated fault: it accumulates, intertwines, creating a chain from which one cannot free oneself alone. This is why deliverance in Christ is so central — only His grace can cut this yoke and unbind the captive. This image of the bound yoke also invites repentance: to recognize that our iniquities have enslaved us.

sens: to stay awake, not to sleep
to monitor attentively, keep an eye on
to be attentive to something or someone
to diligently carry out a task
to be ready to act, to be on the lookout
H8245.detail:
1. To stay awake means not to fall asleep, to remain conscious: "I have no more sleep, and I am like a solitary bird on a roof" (Psalms 102:8) shows one who cannot or does not want to sleep, often due to affliction or concern.
2. To monitor attentively means to maintain control, to protect by staying vigilant: "Be vigilant, and take this under your care" (Ezra 8:29) calls for remaining attentive to what is entrusted.
3. To be attentive to something expresses the sustained intention not to neglect: "Blessed is the man who listens to me, who watches daily at my gates" (Proverbs 8:34) shows one who remains willing and interested, day after day.
4. To diligently carry out a task describes constant engagement in an action: the iniquities that some "watched" to accomplish (Isaiah 29:20) show regular and voluntary work.
5. To be ready to act, to be on the lookout: "he who guards it watches in vain" (Psalms 127:1) evokes the sentinel who remains alert to intervene at any moment.
H8245.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁקַד (shaqad) comes from a root expressing the idea of staying awake, vigilant. The fundamental image is that of the open eye, of maintained awareness. The root evokes the state opposite to sleep: alertness, active guarding. This verb is related to the almond (שָׁקֵד, shaqed in Hebrew), as the almond tree is the first tree to bloom in spring, as if it is always "awake" and attentive to the new season.
H8245.emploi: This verb appears eleven times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and the prophets. It expresses several nuances: the physical vigilance of one who must not sleep (Job 21:32, where the dead "watches" over his grave), the active guarding of a entrusted charge (Ezra 8:29, Psalms 127:1), the sustained attention to something of value (Proverbs 8:34), and the resolute engagement in action, good or bad (Isaiah 29:20, Jeremiah 1:12, 31:28). The meaning nuances according to the context: protective vigilance, devoted attention, or voluntary engagement. God himself "watches" over his word to fulfill it (Jeremiah 1:12).
H8245.portee: This word teaches the believer the importance of spiritual vigilance — not to fall morally asleep, to remain attentive to the voice of God and his commandments. It also reminds that God watches over his word and his people with constant, unwavering faithfulness. The believer who "watches" over the house of God or his teachings never works in vain because God himself watches with him.

sens: Having the shape of an almond (the fruit)
Referring to the ornaments of the gold lampstand in the temple
H8246.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to be almond-shaped" or "to resemble an almond." It is an image based on the characteristic shape of the almond tree's fruit: oblong, slightly pointed at both ends. In Exodus 25:33-34 and 37:19-20, God commands to shape the cups (small vessels) of the gold lampstand of the sanctuary with this precise almond shape, so that the ornament of the temple reflects the beauty and order of creation.
2. The word never designates the fruit itself in the Old Testament: it only qualifies the ritual ornaments of the lampstand. This shape was both aesthetic — recalling nature — and symbolic of purity.
H8246.origine: The Hebrew root שׁקד (shaqad) comes from the observation of the almond tree's fruit, well known in ancient Israel. The word can also mean "to watch" or "to be vigilant" — the almond tree is one of the first trees to bloom in spring, as if it "watches" to announce the new season. The same root appears in the name of the city of Shamir and in the verb that means "to watch attentively."
H8246.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the Bible, all in the description of the gold lampstand (Exodus 25 and 37). It is a technical and liturgical specification: the architects of the ark must copy exactly the design that God shows to Moses on the mountain. This repetition (the same description in Exodus 25 and Exodus 37, which reports the execution of the plan) emphasizes the importance of faithfulness to divine details in worship.
H8246.portee: This word reminds that God cares about details: the beauty, order, and harmony of worship matter to him. The almond-shaped ornaments transform a simple functional object into a symbol of divine creation. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek beauty and precision in the service of God, recognizing that even the details of the temple reflect his glory.

sens: The edible fruit of the almond tree, with its hard shell and nutritious seed
The almond tree itself, the tree that produces this fruit
The bud or flower of the almond tree, particularly in its blooming phase
A biblical symbol or image of vigilance and promptness
H8247.detail:
1. The almond is the edible fruit of the almond tree: a seed protected by a woody shell. In Genesis 43:11, Israel advises his sons to bring almonds as a gift to the Egyptian man, alongside balm and honey, which shows that it was a luxury product, valued and precious in the ancient world.

2. The word also refers to the almond tree, the tree itself. In Ecclesiastes 12:7, the text mentions the almond tree in bloom as a sign of old age: "the almond tree blossoms," an image of life fading and man going to his eternal home.

3. In Numbers 17:8, Aaron's rod "had budded, it had produced blossoms, and it had matured almonds": here the word designates the bud, the flower, and the fruit in development, the plant in its productive cycle that proves divine presence and Aaron's election.

4. Jeremiah's prophetic vision (1:11) associates the almond tree with God's vigilance: "I see a branch of an almond tree," and the Lord replies, "You have seen well; for I am watching over my word to perform it." The almond tree becomes a figure of vigilance, perhaps because it blooms earlier than other trees and remains alert to the changing seasons.
H8247.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to watch" or "to be vigilant," which explains why the almond tree is associated with divine surveillance in Jeremiah's vision. In nature, the almond tree was already known and cultivated in Egypt and the ancient Near East; it is one of the first trees to bloom in spring, which may have reinforced its symbolic link with vigilance and promptness.
H8247.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, in very diverse contexts. First as a luxury fruit offered as a gift (Genesis 43:11). Then, it takes on liturgical and theological importance: Aaron's rod buds with almonds (Numbers 17:8), which authenticates his priestly role before Israel. Ecclesiastes mentions it as a poetic image of aging (12:7). Finally, in Jeremiah 1:11, the almond tree becomes the object of a prophetic vision that seals the divine message. In each usage, the word oscillates between its botanical reality and its symbolic charge: vigilance, election, spiritual productivity, proximity to the end.
H8247.portee: When God shows Jeremiah the almond tree and says to him, "I am watching," the prophet and the reader learn that God is never asleep: his word will be fulfilled according to his plan. Aaron's rod that blooms with almonds teaches that spiritual legitimacy comes from God alone, not from appearances or human strength. These two images remind us that we serve a vigilant God, attentive, whose power often manifests in unexpected and miraculous ways.

sens: Pour water a plant or the soil to make it grow
Give water to an animal
Soak, saturate
Provide with water, irrigate a field
Meet someone's vital needs in a figurative sense
H8248G.detail:
1. Watering means pouring water on a plant or the soil so that it grows. It is the action of the gardener who cultivates: in Genesis 2:6, a mist "watered the whole surface of the ground" so that vegetation could come to life. In a concrete sense, it refers to the systematic irrigation of a field, as in Deuteronomy 11:10, where it was necessary to "water" the fields of Egypt by foot (that is, through a hydraulic system).

2. Giving water to an animal means providing it with something to drink. In Genesis 24:46, the servant "watered" the camels at the pitcher. It is an act of hospitality and care for the animals: in Exodus 2:16, the daughters of the priest of Midian filled the troughs to "water their father's flock."

3. In a figurative sense, watering means soaking or saturating something. The rain "waters" the mountains in Psalms 104:13, meaning it envelops and nourishes them with its drops; the whole earth is "satisfied" by it.

4. The word can more broadly refer to the action of providing water, irrigating. A well-watered field is a fertile land; a watered flock is a flock whose needs are met.

5. On a spiritual level, watering represents the act of nourishing, supporting, providing. God "waters" His people like one waters a precious plant that is cultivated (Isaiah 27:3).
H8248G.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁקָה (shaqah) comes from a root that expresses the act of pouring or spilling a liquid. The word evokes the image of the shepherd or the farmer who quenches thirst, who moistens the earth. In the same family, there are words related to drinking and hydration. In both Hebrew and Greek of the Old Testament, this verb is common to describe the vital action of providing water, whether for animals or plants.
H8248G.emploi: The verb שָׁקָה appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mostly found in the narratives of Genesis (stories of wells and watering livestock) and in poetic texts (Psalms, Ecclesiastes). In Genesis, the context is almost always pastoral or agricultural: watering flocks at the well, irrigating fields. The Psalms and the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel) use it in a more figurative manner: God "waters" the mountains, He "waters" His vineyard, meaning He sustains and protects it. The verb thus carries a meaning that evolves from the concrete (giving water) to the spiritual (nourishing, protecting).
H8248G.portee: This word reminds us that the Lord provides for our vital needs: He "waters" His people like a shepherd waters his flock. It is a beautiful image of His tender and constant Providence. For us, recognizing that we have been "watered" by His grace means accepting our dependence on Him and living in gratitude. The word also invites us to imitate this benevolent vigilance towards others: watering the thirsty is to perform an act of love and mercy.

sens: Give something to drink, make drink
Offer water or a drink to someone or an animal
Figuratively: irrigate or water a land
Figuratively: satisfy, fill someone with something
Figuratively: make someone absorb, impose something bad
H8248H.detail:
1. Giving someone a drink, offering them a beverage: it is an act of generosity and care. Rebecca gives water to Abraham's servant and his camels (Genesis 24:19), and later she feeds and gives them drink (2 Chronicles 28:15).
2. Giving water to animals, allowing them to quench their thirst: one can water the household animals so they do not die of thirst.
3. Watering or irrigating a land, making it fertile by moistening it: it is the image of water that gives life to plants and fields.
4. Satisfying someone with goods or blessings, filling them as one fills a glass: God gives His people His goodness (Psalms 36:9).
5. Making someone absorb a bad or bitter drink, forcing them to drink something harmful: Jeremiah announces that God will make His people drink poisoned waters (Jeremiah 23:15), or make someone drink wine to deceive them (Genesis 19:32).
H8248H.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that designates the action of giving water. The word also appears in forms that indicate a more passive action (being given water) or a relationship of irrigation. It is a very common verb in ancient Hebrew texts, both in the literal and figurative sense: it always speaks of water entering the body or the close contact of a person or land with water.
H8248H.emploi: The verb appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis, the Psalms, and the prophetic books. In its literal sense, it denotes the very concrete action of giving drink to a person or an animal (Rebecca and the camels in Genesis 24, the captives rescued in 2 Chronicles 28:15). In a figurative sense, it expresses how God gives His people blessings or His promises (Psalms 36:9, 60:5), or how He forces them to drink the bitterness of judgment (Jeremiah 23:15, 25:15). The image of water becoming poison or bitterness also marks the curse or punishment (Numbers 5:24-27). Finally, it is an act of charity towards the enemy (Proverbs 25:21).
H8248H.portee: This word reminds us that mercy comes through simple gestures: giving drink to the thirsty is recognizing their need and relieving it. It also shows that God gives His people blessings, but can also make them drink the bitterness of judgment if infidelity compels Him to do so. It is a word that calls the believer to generosity towards others, even towards their enemies.

sens: Pour or add a substance to a drink
Mix tears with what one drinks
Figuratively: contaminate or alter something by adding a painful element
H8249.detail:
1. The word describes the action of pouring or incorporating something into a drink to transform it. It is the material act of mixing two liquids together. In Psalms 102:10, the psalmist says he "mixes tears with his drink": he adds his tears to what he drinks, a poignant image of his distress.
2. Specifically, the word evokes the act of pouring one's tears into one's drink, creating a bitter and contaminated beverage. This biblical image expresses how emotional pain invades even the ordinary acts of sustenance. The psalmist can no longer eat or drink normally: everything has become an expression of his affliction.
3. Figuratively, "mixing" represents how suffering infiltrates and blends into all of existence. The tears are not poured separately: they enter every sip, symbolizing a sorrow that permeates all of life.
H8249.origine: The word שִׁקֻּו belongs to the family of שִׁקּוּי (shiq.quy), which comes from the root meaning "to drink" or "to give drink." This root expresses the idea of a beverage or the absorption of liquid. The word here specifically designates the action of preparing or mixing a drink, making it drinkable or altering it.
H8249.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 102:10, a psalm of supplication where the poet expresses his deep anguish. In this context, "mixing tears with his drink" translates not only a physical act — pouring one's tears into what one drinks — but also symbolically describes how pain invades everything, even basic needs. It is a raw and touching image of human distress brought before God.
H8249.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that suffering can sometimes be so deep that it contaminates all daily existence. At the same time, the psalmist brings this distress before God in prayer: mixing his tears with his drink is not a hidden shame, it is a cry that God hears. It speaks to anyone going through a prolonged trial and feeling overwhelmed.

sens: What one drinks to quench thirst and refresh oneself
Material help and support received from others
H8250.detail:
1. The word primarily designates literally a drink — what one consumes. In Hosea 2:7, a woman lists what she receives from her lovers: "my bread and my water, my wool and my linen, my oil and my drink" — she speaks of the essentials of life.
2. By extension, it takes on the meaning of "refreshment," something that restores and comforts the body. In Proverbs 3:8, the text promises that wisdom "will be health to your flesh and refreshment to your bones": we see how drink symbolizes here everything that restores strength and vigor.
H8250.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of drinking and quenching thirst. It belongs to the family of words related to drink and nourishment: what enters the body to feed and restore it. The image is concrete and immediate: that of water or wine brought to one's mouth.
H8250.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in Proverbs 3:8, where refreshment is the beneficial effect of wisdom on the whole body. Then in Hosea 2:7, where it is included in the list of material goods (bread, water, wool, linen, oil) that the adulterous woman receives from her partners. In both cases, the dominant idea is: something that sustains, restores, supports life. The context of Hosea places it in a human relationship; that of Proverbs in the realm of wisdom and health.
H8250.portee: This word shows how material needs — to eat, to drink — are at the heart of human life and dependence. In Hosea, it reminds us that the woman seeks from creatures what she should seek from God. In Proverbs, it teaches us that God's wisdom is not just a matter of the mind: it heals and strengthens even to the marrow of the bones. Drink thus becomes an image of everything that supports and invigorates us.

sens: That which inspires disgust and horror, particularly in religious matters
Object of idolatrous worship, statue or representation of a false deity
Practice or behavior that violates God's law and defiles those who approach it
That which profanes a sacred place when introduced there
Something so repugnant that it brings upon itself divine judgment
H8251.detail:
1. An abomination is primarily something that evokes disgust and horror. It particularly designates what is morally and religiously repugnant in the eyes of God. In Deuteronomy 29:17, the people see the "abominations" of the neighboring nations — their statues and idols — and understand that these are detestable things, far from the holiness of the Lord.
2. An abomination is often an idol, a carved or molten image intended to represent a foreign deity. When Ezekiel 5:11 speaks of "idols" and "abominations," it refers to these material objects that draw hearts away from the true God and defile those who honor them.
3. The word also designates the act of worshiping these false gods or practicing the accompanying cults. Such behaviors are an abomination because they violate the first law given by God: "You shall have no other gods before me." Ezekiel 20:7 exhorts the people to reject "the abominations that draw your eyes."
4. An abomination can be introduced into a holy place and profane it. Jeremiah 7:30 recounts that the children of Judah placed their abominations "in the house upon which my name is called, to defile it" — the Temple itself becomes a place of spiritual contamination.
5. Finally, an abomination is something so repugnant that it provokes divine judgment. Daniel 9:27 mentions the "most abominable things" committed in the sanctuary, acts that lead to ruin and desolation.
H8251.origine: The Hebrew word shiq.quts comes from a root that means "to smell bad, to feel disgust." It is related to the physical idea of repulsion and nausea. The same root produces verbs expressing horror and aversion. The word has a strong emotional force: it does not simply describe a disagreement or an error, but a visceral repulsion, the kind that God Himself feels towards idolatry and impure practices. It is a word particularly frequent among the prophets, who use it to express God's disgust at the people's unfaithfulness.
H8251.emploi: The word shiq.quts appears 26 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books. It is concentrated in Ezekiel (who uses it about 12 times to describe the idols and impure practices of the people), Jeremiah, and Daniel. Deuteronomy and Leviticus use it to qualify the idols of the nations and the impure ritual acts. In Ezekiel, an abomination is primarily an idol or an act of idolatrous worship that defiles the person and the Temple; the prophet calls the people to reject them (Ezekiel 20:7-8). In Jeremiah, the abomination is often an act — placing idols in the Temple (7:30), multiplying unfaithfulness (13:27) — that provokes the Lord's anger. Daniel uses it to designate the profanations of the sanctuary and religious persecutions (9:27, 11:31, 12:11), images of desolation that attract judgment. The word thus oscillates between the idolatrous object (the idol itself) and the act or practice that accompanies it.
H8251.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God hates everything that diverts Him from Himself. An abomination is not simply a mistake or a weakness: it is a rupture of relationship, an unfaithfulness that provokes God's horror. The word invites us to examine our own lives and identify what may have become an idol — wealth, ambition, pleasure — and to reject it with the same firmness that the people of Israel should have rejected the idols. It is a call to holiness and purity of heart.

sens: State of calm, absence of noise or movement
State of peace, absence of conflict or threat
Inactivity, cessation of action
Absence of anger or emotional agitation
Inner tranquility, serenity of mind
H8252.detail:
1. Rest primarily means physical calm: the absence of noise, movement, or disturbance. When Joshua conquers the land, "the land had rest" (Joshua 11:23) — there are no more wars, no more agitation, no more conflicts shaking it. It is a concrete, lasting peace.

2. Rest also refers to political and social peace: the absence of conflict between peoples or kingdoms. During the wars of the Judges, when the Lord grants victory, "the land had rest" for forty years (Judges 3:11, 3:30) — the enemies are defeated, the borders are secure, and the inhabitants can live without fear.

3. Rest can also mean inactivity or abstention: to cease acting, to cease waging war, to cease pursuing a goal. Isaiah says, "I will not take rest" (Isaiah 62:1) — he refuses to stop his intercession for Jerusalem.

4. Rest expresses emotional calm, the peace of the heart in the face of fear. The prophet says to the king of Judah: "Be calm, do not fear, and let not your heart be troubled" (Isaiah 7:4) — it is an invitation to let go of anxiety, to regain confidence despite the threat.

5. Finally, rest can signify the deep serenity of the Lord who controls history: when God "gives rest, who can cause trouble?" (Job 34:29) — it is the tranquility of one who knows that nothing escapes God's hand.
H8252.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁקַט comes from a root that evokes the idea of stretching out, settling down without moving, like someone who rests after fatigue. This idea is found in contexts where one "rests" (Ruth 3:18: "The woman will rest quietly"). The root fundamentally expresses the transition from movement and agitation to calm and stability. It is a common word throughout the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the historical books and the Psalms.
H8252.emploi: The verb שָׁקַט appears 41 times in the Hebrew biblical text. It is mainly used in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) to describe periods of peace between Israel's wars. In the Psalms and Isaiah, its meaning deepens: it is less about the simple absence of conflict than the peace of the heart before God, or the tranquility that only God can give. In Jeremiah, it sometimes takes on a nuance of warning: a false tranquility that ignores God's judgment (Jeremiah 48:11 describes the Moabites "who rested on their lees," without fearing change). The word also plays on the idea of cessation: to cease fighting, to cease complaining, to cease walking — thus translating the Hebrew as "rest," "quiet," or "calm" depending on the context.
H8252.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that only the Lord can give true peace, one that does not depend on circumstances. When the Bible calls to be "calm" in the face of threat (Isaiah 7:4), it teaches trust in God who orders history. Conversely, the rest that the people seek in forgetting God becomes unstable and false. It is a word that speaks to the heart of the Christian: how to find true peace, not by fleeing conflicts, but by resting in God.

sens: State of peace and absence of trouble
Rest far from battles and enemies
Inner calm and security of the heart
H8253.detail:
1. Tranquility is the state of one who lives in peace, without agitation or torment. It is the opposite of chaos and violence. When God promises Solomon that he will be born as "a man of rest" and will receive rest, it is this tranquility that God offers him (1 Chronicles 22:9).
2. It concretely means the absence of conflicts and military threats. Israel will know peace and tranquility during Solomon's reign because God "will deliver him from all his surrounding enemies": no more enemies, no more wars, thus calm and security.
3. Beyond the political and military context, it also denotes inner rest, the serenity of one who has nothing to fear and can live without tension.
H8253.origine: The Hebrew word sheqet comes from a root that expresses the idea of remaining calm, sitting in peace. It describes the state of stability and rest, the absence of agitated movement. It is the image of a person or a people who can finally sit down safely, breathe without fear.
H8253.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 22:9, in the mouth of David speaking to his son Solomon. David explains that unlike him, who has waged war all his life, Solomon will be "a man of rest" to whom God will grant tranquility: Israel will no longer be at war, the enemies will be defeated, and the land will know a period of peace. It is a divine gift, a blessing linked to wisdom and obedience.
H8253.portee: This promise of tranquility reminds believers that only God can give true peace: not the absence of all problems, but a peace based on deliverance, protection, and trust in God. It shows that the rest God promises is not vain idleness, but a precious gift granted to the faithful people.

sens: Determine the weight of something by placing it on a scale
Count and hand over a sum of money by weighing it (as gold and silver were weighed to assess their value)
Evaluate, examine something seriously
Carry a weight, be heavy (figuratively: be a burden to the mind)
H8254.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to place something on a scale to know its weight. It is the action of the merchant or collector who must evaluate a commodity. Isaiah 40:12 gives the grandest image when it asks who has "weighed the mountains in a balance."

2. In the ancient economic context, where currency is not minted but consists of raw metal, "weighing" means counting gold or silver by placing it on the scale and then handing it over to someone. It is the means of payment: Abraham "weighs" four hundred shekels of silver to Ephron (Genesis 23:16), Ezra "hands over" six hundred fifty talents of silver by weighing them (Ezra 8:26).

3. The verb can also mean to evaluate, to weigh a question, a decision thoughtfully. It is the careful examination of a matter, as one examines the weight of something.

4. Rarely, in metaphorical language, "weighing" expresses the heaviness of suffering or responsibility that burdens the mind, what "weighs" on the heart.
H8254.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁקל comes from a root evoking the action of lifting, holding in balance on a scale. The noun שֶׁקֶל (sheqel), one of the units of weight and later the Hebrew currency, comes from this same verb: it is literally "what has been weighed." The original imagery is that of the scale and balance. This verb and its monetary derivatives testify to the importance of weighing in the ancient economy, where transactions in precious metal relied on weighing rather than on stamped coins.
H8254.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in commercial or administrative contexts. In the times of the patriarchs and kings, it is the common means of payment: Abraham and Jeremiah weigh money to buy a field. In the accounts of the kings (2 Samuel, 1 Kings), tributes or wages are weighed. Ezra reports that enormous quantities of treasures were weighed for the temple. The verb is also used figuratively to express comparisons: Job reflects on what cannot be bought "at the weight of money" (Job 28:15). Isaiah uses it poetically to assert that God weighs even the mountains. The passage in Zechariah 11:12 about the thirty pieces of silver shows the verb in a precise transaction context.
H8254.portee: This verb reminds us that trust and honesty are at the heart of commerce and covenant. Weighing justly means refusing deception and recognizing true value. Spiritually, weighing also evokes God's judgment, who "weighs" hearts and actions (a notion developed by other Hebrew words): He evaluates what is true and lasting, far from appearances.

sens: Unit of weight used to measure precious metals (gold, silver, copper)
Currency of value, used as a means of exchange and payment
Reference measure for religious contributions and redemptions
H8255.detail:
1. The shekel is primarily a unit of weight. Depending on its material, its value varies: a silver shekel weighs about 11 grams, a gold shekel proportionally more (Exodus 38:29 mentions bronze shekels among the materials of the tabernacle). It is the standard measure of the ancient Near East for weighing gold and silver in significant transactions.

2. As currency, the shekel becomes the standard monetary unit of Israel. Payments are made in silver shekels: Abraham purchases a tomb for four hundred silver shekels (Genesis 23:15), and King Menahem imposes a tax of fifty shekels per person (2 Kings 15:20). This is equivalent to several days' wages.

3. For sacred offerings, the sanctuary shekel is the official measure. Each Israelite contributes a half-shekel for the upkeep of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:13), and redemptions of children or animals are calculated in shekels according to fixed tables (Leviticus 27:3-7). It is the reference weight for religious purposes.
H8255.origine: The Hebrew word sheqel comes from a root meaning "to weigh." Its Aramaic equivalent is teqel. Originally, it literally means "that which weighs" (a weighed object), as before the minting of coins, gold or silver ingots were exchanged by weighing them on a scale. The word has been borrowed by Greek, Latin, and other languages, as the shekel was well-known in ancient economies.
H8255.emploi: The word appears 54 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Pentateuch and Kings. Genesis 23 and Exodus 30 establish it as a commercial and religious standard. Exodus 38 uses it to weigh the materials of the tabernacle. Leviticus 27 sets the redemption rates in shekels: 50 shekels for a man, 30 for a woman, proportionally less for children. Numbers 3 and 7 use it for contributions and offerings during the dedication of the altar. In 2 Kings 15:20, it designates the tax imposed on each Israelite. 1 Samuel 17:5 mentions the weight of Goliath's armor in shekels. The context varies: private transactions, taxes, sacred offerings, redemptions, value estimations.
H8255.portee: The shekel reminds the reader that in the Bible, the price of things—a human life, an offering to the temple, access to divine service—is measured concretely and justly. It shows that God does not disdain economic order and that worship has a material and communal dimension. The rates in Leviticus 27 also reveal a certain equity: reductions for the poor (Leviticus 27:8). Finally, the sanctuary shekel, distinct from common currency, symbolizes that the relationship with God adheres to its own criteria, not to market fluctuations.

sens: Common fruit tree in Egypt and the Levant, bearing edible figs
Wood from this tree, used in construction and carpentry
Abundance or material prosperity, when this tree is numerous
H8256.detail:
1. The sycamore is a robust tree that grows in the warm plains of the Near East, particularly in Egypt and Canaan. It produces fruits resembling figs, which serve as food. Amos, for example, describes himself as someone who cultivates and harvests sycamores (Amos 7:14), a humble yet useful task.

2. The wood of the sycamore, hard and durable, was highly valued for construction and furniture making. The text of 1 Chronicles 27:28 mentions the one who supervised the sycamores in the royal plain, indicating that the king owned entire plantations managed by servants.

3. The abundance of sycamores symbolizes the wealth and prosperity of a nation at peace. When Solomon made "silver and gold as common as stones" and "cedars as numerous as sycamores in the plain" (1 Kings 10:27; 2 Chronicles 1:15), he expressed extraordinary prosperity. Conversely, when God destroys the sycamores with hail and frost (Psalms 78:47), or when they are deliberately cut down to be replaced by more prestigious cedars (Isaiah 9:9), it signals the humiliation and rebuilding of Israel.
H8256.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁקְמָה (shiqmah) likely comes from an ancient root referring to this Mediterranean tree well-known to Egyptians and Canaanites. It is a borrowing or adaptation from an older Semitic language. The sycamore was so familiar to the Hebrews that there is no doubt about the identification of this plant in biblical texts.
H8256.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of wealth, economic production, or divine punishment. It is mostly found in the accounts of Solomon's splendor (1 Kings 10:27; 2 Chronicles 1:15 and 9:27), where the abundance of sycamores illustrates the prosperity of the kingdom. It also appears in prophetic texts: Isaiah mentions it during threats of destruction (9:9), while Psalms 78:47 refers to it among the plagues inflicted on Egypt and Israel. Amos 7:14 is the only passage where an individual (not a king) works with sycamores, revealing their cultivation across all levels of society.
H8256.portee: The sycamore reminds readers that material wealth and prosperity are gifts from God and not eternal guarantees. It is an "ordinary" tree, less noble than the cedar, but useful and abundant: it invites valuing humble and daily work. Finally, its fate—prosperity or destruction depending on the faithfulness of the people—illustrates that God controls even nature to punish or reward His people.

sens: To gradually descend, to submerge
To lose stability, to collapse
To gradually decrease, to calm down
H8257.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: something sinks or descends. This is what the crocodile describes in Job 40:20: its tongue can be "grasped" by weight, it sinks. More dramatically, Babylon in Jeremiah 51:64 will be "submerged" by calamities, it will sink without being able to rise again.

2. The verb also describes the collapse of a structure or terrain. In Amos 8:8 and 9:5, the earth itself "sinks" like the waters of the Nile during the flood: it rises, then gradually falls, unstable and shaken.

3. By extension, the word also expresses the calming or diminishing of agitation. In Ezekiel 32:14, the waters "calm down"; they lose their violence. In Numbers 11:2, the fire "stops": it ceases to progress, its action is interrupted.
H8257.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that paints the image of something tipping, losing its balance and descending. The word evokes the natural force of gravity: what rises must come down. The same root appears in other contexts where one speaks of sinking or submerging in waters.
H8257.emploi: This verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos) and in the accounts of Job and Numbers. Translations vary according to context: "stop" when the fire ceases, "grasp" when the crocodile sinks, "submerged" for a city engulfed by calamity, "calm" for the waters that settle, "sink" for the earth that collapses. The verb always carries an idea of downward movement or loss of stability, but the context guides the translation.
H8257.portee: This word reminds of the instability of worldly things: the earth trembles, the water rises and falls, empires sink. For the believer, it illustrates how the Lord masters forces that seem uncontrollable—He can stop the fire, calm the waters, make Babylon sink. It is an invitation to trust in the One who governs even the elements of creation.

sens: Hollow or indentation in a surface
Depression where something can form or accumulate
H8258.detail:
1. The word refers to a hollow, a visible indentation in a surface – here the walls of a house. It is a depression that stands out in relief: it appears more recessed than the rest (Leviticus 14:37).
2. A cavity can be the place where things accumulate or settle – such as mold or forms of leprosy that eat away at the stone and leave hollow marks.
H8258.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of indentation and hollow. It is a rare nominal form used to describe what is literally dug or depressed in a solid material. The image is that of a surface that yields, that slightly collapses.
H8258.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 14:37. It is used in the diagnosis of leprosy in houses according to the Law: the priest examines the walls to detect abnormal cavities, greenish or reddish, which signal the presence of the disease. It is a technical and very precise term in the ritual vocabulary of purity.
H8258.portee: This word reminds us that the Law of Moses does not overlook any detail: it touches on all areas of life, including the hygiene of dwellings. Cavities in the walls are not merely an aesthetic flaw, but a sign of God's judgment on disease. This invites us to consider the house as a space under the gaze of the Creator.

sens: Look from a high point downwards
Examine attentively, observe
Lean to see or consider
Direct one's gaze towards someone or something with a particular intention
H8259.detail:
1. Look from a high point downwards: it is primarily a physical gaze cast from above. When God "looks" from the heavens, He encompasses everything with His dominating gaze. In Genesis 18:16, the three men "look towards Sodom" from the height where they stand, and in 2 Samuel 6:16, Michal observes through her window, from a position that allows her to see without being seen.

2. Examine attentively, observe: the word is not a mere passing glance, but a concentrated observation. The Lord "looks" at the camp of the Egyptians in Exodus 14:24 with an attention that leads to a decisive action — He brings confusion. Similarly, in Psalms 14:2 and 53:3, God "looks at the sons of men" to evaluate their wisdom and their seeking of Him.

3. Lean to see or consider: the word often implies an inclination, a benevolent attention. When the psalmist pleads with God, "look from Your holy dwelling" (Deuteronomy 26:15), he asks God to actively turn towards Israel, like someone who leans in with intention. The gaze is never distant or indifferent.

4. Direct one's gaze towards someone or something with a particular intention: it is a gaze that judges, evaluates, acts. In 2 Kings 9:32, the eunuchs "look" through the window at the man who cries out to them. This is not merely seeing; it is considering with a purpose: to recognize, assess, intervene.
H8259.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of leaning or bending forward to see. The image is of someone climbing to a height, leaning, and looking down — hence the central idea of "looking from a dominant position." This elevated position gives the gaze a particular strength: it is not an equal gaze, but one that discovers, watches, judges from above. The different verbal forms (to look simply, or to cause someone to look) allow for the expression of both divine observation and human observation.
H8259.emploi: The verb appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to describe how God or a person in a high position (physically or morally) observes what is below. God "looks" at humans from above (Psalms 14:2, 53:3), or looks intentionally at a people in danger (Exodus 14:24, Deuteronomy 26:15). Humans "look" through a window (2 Samuel 6:16, 2 Kings 9:32), from a citadel (Judges 5:28), or from a height (Genesis 19:28, Numbers 21:20). The word is also used to "look at" a woman with appreciation (Song of Solomon 6:10). In all cases, it combines the idea of a favorable position and attentive observation, never indifferent.
H8259.portee: This word reminds us that God "looks" at the world from a height where He sees everything. Unlike our limited gaze, His is never superficial or distracted — He observes to understand, to act, to judge justly. This invites the believer to meditate on the reality of this vigilant presence of God: nothing escapes His gaze. It should also transform our own way of looking at others: not with disdain from above, but with the benevolent attention of one who desires to understand and help.

sens: Structure of wood or stone that forms the frame of a door or window
Set of beams that make up the framework or structure of a building
H8260.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the structure of wood or stone that frames an opening (door or window), that is, what supports and borders the access. In 1 Kings 7:5, Solomon builds buildings where "all the doors and all the posts were made of square beams": this refers to the uprights and lintels that make up the rigid frame of each door. 2. More broadly, the word can refer to the structural elements in wood that form the framework or skeleton of a construction, the main pieces that support the edifice and maintain its shape.
H8260.origine: This Hebrew word is related to the idea of what stands or rises, of what forms a solid frame. It comes from a root evoking the tension or rigidity of a structure. The word is akin to other Hebrew terms designating architectural elements, all centered on the idea of a framework or armature.
H8260.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 7:5, in the context of the constructions built by Solomon. It precisely describes the beams that frame the doors of the buildings he built with his architects. Its unique usage places it among the technical and specialized terms of biblical architecture, specific to the narration of the great works of Solomon's reign.
H8260.portee: For the Christian reader, this detail about the construction of Solomon's palace reminds us of the wisdom and power of the king — everything is ordered, regular, "square beams", symmetrical. It is an image of the order and beauty that mark God's work in the believer's heart.

sens: Frame or casing of a window
Grid or barred structure enclosing an opening
What securely closes or holds
H8261.detail:
1. The word refers to the frame or casing of a window — the wooden or metal structure that encases the opening and holds the glass or panels. In 1 Kings 6:4, the king ordered "strongly grilled windows": this refers to a tight lattice that allows light to enter while securing access.
2. More generally, it is a perforated but sturdy structure, composed of bars or interwoven strips that form a regular pattern. This type of construction allows for both ventilation and protection, very useful in a temple or palace.
3. The underlying image is that of something that "holds firmly": the word describes what frames, contains, and secures the opening.
H8261.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁקוּף (shaquph) comes from a root expressing the idea of "looking through" or "seeing through an opening." It is related to words that denote the action of piercing or creating an opening. The word thus evokes both the opening of the window and the structure that borders and consolidates it.
H8261.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible (1 Kings 6:4 and 7:4), both concerning the temple of Solomon. In both cases, it describes the windows of the temple: in 1 Kings 6:4, the text speaks of "strongly grilled windows," suggesting a tight and sturdy lattice. The context shows that these are architectural details of the sacred building, designed to let in light while maintaining the security and dignity of the place.
H8261.portee: This word reminds us that even the architectural details of Solomon's temple reflect divine wisdom and mastery. The mention of these grilled windows invites the reader to contemplate the beauty and solidity of God's house, built with care and intention.

sens: To feel intense repulsion, disgust for something or someone
To declare something or someone as detestable, forbidden, impure
To make oneself impure or detestable through a wrongful act
H8262.detail:
1. Abominate means to have a horror of, to experience a deep aversion. It is the feeling that Israel must have towards certain animals: "You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat their flesh" (Leviticus 11:11). It is a disgust that drives one to reject, to absolutely refuse.
2. The word also refers to the act of declaring something abominable or detestable — that is, contaminated, forbidden by the law. God lists the animals "that you shall regard as detestable" (Leviticus 11:13), separating them from the clean animals that can be eaten.
3. Abominate can also mean to make oneself abominable or impure: "Do not make yourselves detestable by any swarming thing that swarms" (Leviticus 11:43). It is less about the feeling than the action — that of voluntarily defiling oneself, transgressing the order established by God.
H8262.origine: This Hebrew verb fundamentally expresses the idea of forcefully pushing away, rejecting. It belongs to the vocabulary of ritual purity in Israel: an abominable animal is one that must be turned away from. The root evokes both physical and moral disgust — the instinctive rejection of what is impure or deviant. It is a key word in the Mosaic Law for distinguishing the permitted from the forbidden.
H8262.emploi: The verb appears about 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in Leviticus (the law concerning clean and unclean foods). It is first used to qualify feelings towards forbidden animals: Israel must "abominate" them. Then the meaning broadens: to abominate someone is also to treat them with contempt or disdain (Psalms 22:25, where Christ affirms that God does not disdain the suffering). The word always expresses a radical separation — a rejection that reflects the divine will for distinction between the clean and the unclean, the permitted and the forbidden.
H8262.portee: This verb teaches the reader the biblical notion of holiness: to be holy is to make distinctions, to reject what defiles. But it also invites vigilance: abomination is not just an emotion, it is an act — do not make oneself impure. For the Christian, this speaks of moral discernment and separation from evil, not out of pharisaical disgust, but out of love for the purity established by God.

sens: That which provokes disgust and physical repulsion
That which is ritually impure and forbidden for consumption
That which is morally repugnant and contrary to the will of God
That which is destined for destruction and absolute rejection
H8263.detail:
1. The word primarily designates something that provokes disgust: an impure animal to look at, a creature whose body inspires horror. In Leviticus 11:10-12, God lists aquatic creatures — those without fins or scales — as "abominations": the mere sight of them is nauseating.
2. It is also religious impurity: these animals cannot be eaten because they violate the boundary between the clean and the unclean that God has drawn for His people. Eating their flesh makes one impure before God. It is a legal category as much as a visceral repulsion (Leviticus 11:11).
3. In a moral and spiritual sense, the word extends to anything that offends God: idols, impious practices. It is God's own disgust in the face of sin and unfaithfulness (Ezekiel 8:10).
4. The word finally carries the meaning of total condemnation: what is an abomination deserves to be annihilated, cast out, rejected without mercy.
H8263.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of turning away, rejecting. An abomination is literally the thing before which one turns away, that which cannot be looked at without repulsion. It evokes a physical and moral reaction, a recoil in the face of the foul or the wicked.
H8263.emploi: The word appears mainly in Leviticus (11 occurrences), where God lists the animals that the people of Israel must regard as abominations: fish, birds, reptiles (Leviticus 11:10-23). It is the law of the clean and the unclean, foundational to Israel's religious identity. It is also found in Isaiah 66:17 and Ezekiel 8:10, where the term moves beyond dietary matters to denounce idolatrous practices and impious worship. In all cases, abomination marks an inviolable boundary: it is what must absolutely not be done, not eaten, not worshiped.
H8263.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God draws clear boundaries between the clean and the unclean, the permitted and the forbidden. Although the Levitical laws on food no longer bind the believer of the New Testament, this word retains its force: it warns us that certain things are repugnant to God, and that idolatry and sin inspire Him with deep disgust. It is an invitation to cultivate the same revulsion towards evil and impurity.

sens: To run swiftly, to move with impetuosity
To charge ardently or violently at something
To be eager, thirsty, hungry for something
To go back and forth hastily, to agitate feverishly
H8264.detail:
1. The primary sense describes a rapid and energetic movement: to run, to launch oneself, to charge. It is the image of the locust rushing towards its prey (Isaiah 33:4) or soldiers running on the walls (Joel 2:9).
2. This movement can be tinged with aggressiveness or covetousness: to throw oneself upon something with violence and desire. The wicked "hungry" (literally: rushing, charging) dominates the weak like a bear charging (Proverbs 28:15).
3. The verb also expresses intense desire, thirst, hunger. The "thirsty" soul is one that longs for water; the "fainting" soul (Isaiah 29:8) is one that consumes with desire, like someone who dreams of drinking but wakes up thirsty.
H8264.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁקק comes from a root that paints impetuous movement and appetite: roving (wandering, running here and there), rushing (charging), and longing (aspiring, languishing). This same root expresses both violent physical movement and the intensity of desire — two forms of the same force that pushes, that drives.
H8264.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Joel, Nahum) and in Psalms and Proverbs. It depicts either the assault of enemies rushing upon the city (Joel, Nahum) or the violent appetite (hungry, thirsty) of a predator or a being in desire. When the verb qualifies hunger or thirst, it emphasizes an intense physical desire, almost a restlessness of the entire body.
